speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer a question put on March 22 by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) as to the intention of the government with respect to objectives set out in the joint statement on Trieste issued on Saturday, March 20. by the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and France. The first part of this declaration reads as follows:
The governments of the United States, United Kingdom and France have proposed to the governments of the Soviet Union and Italy that those governments join in agreement on an additional protocol to the treaty of peace with Italy which would place the free territory of Trieste once more under Italian sovereignty.
In his address before the plenary session of the Paris conference on August 2, 1946, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
Our concern as a nation is to see that, as far as we can help to make them so, the peace treaties will be based upon broad and enduring principles of justice and equity. Canada seeks no territory, no reparations, no special concessions of any kind, but we do seek to build a lasting peace.
On October 8, 1946, the head of the Canadian delegation, the Hon. Brooke Claxton, speaking before the plenary conference, stated with reference to the statute of Trieste:
The compromise for which the large majority of the commission eventually voted followed the lines laid down by the council of foreign ministers. The Canadian delegation supported the creation of the free territory of Trieste in the hope that it will possess genuine independence under the authority of the united nations. This hope, however, is based upon the belief that in the last resort Yugoslavia, which was in the forefront in the Avar against the axis forces, will find it possible to play a leading role in supporting a pacific and progressive solution of this most difficult aspect of the Italian settlement.
This hope has not been realized. In reply to the question of the hon. member for Peel, therefore, I wish to state that it is the intention of the Canadian government to support the proposal of the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom, and France to return the free territory of Trieste to Italy by revision of the peace treaty with Italy.

Does that mean that the resolution standing on the order paper in the name of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as the second order under government notices of motion will have to be amended with respect to Italy?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. It is our intention to proceed with this resolution, and, if there is a protocol to the Italian peace treaty, to bring it forward in proper time for approval by the house.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 30, the board of transport commissioners brought down its decision on the application of the railways for permission to increase their rates by thirty per cent. It will be recalled that they also asked that on coal a flat rate or sliding scale of rates of increase be permitted. According to the judgment of the board, the railway companies are authorized to publish and file tariff schedules in accordance with the board's findings on not less than three days' notice. The minimum charge for single less than carload shipments between any two stations will be one hundred pounds at first class rate, but not less than seventy-five cents. Then they go on to say that the recognized differentials via rail, water and rail routes are to be preserved as far as may be practicable, even though certain rates via differential routes may be lower or higher than would otherwise prevail if such rates were subjected to the increase authorized. As hon. members no doubt know from reading the judgment issued by the board, the increase 'authorized is a flat increase across the board of 21 per cent, together with an increase of 25 cents a ton on coal.
There are of course certain exceptions to this increase which the board has listed, namely, rates affected by the Crowsnest Pass agreement, the rates on the movement of grain, feeds and so on east and west, and the rates which are affected by our relations with the United States and the transportation systems of the two countries.
The proposed increase in freight rates I take it is a matter of vital concern to every part of Canada. It is of particular concern to certain parts of Canada, namely, the maritime provinces, the Pacific coast province of British Columbia and the provinces that we call the prairie provinces. This is a flat increase in rates of 21 per cent across the board-in other words, .a horizontal increase, as it was sometimes termed in the discussions before the board of transport commissioners. I think it should be noted that all the interests in the regions to which I have referred, whether governmental, * commercial, agricultural, or otherwise are united .in opposition to this increase in freight rates.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that the implications of these increases are a matter of grave concern to this house and to the country at the present time, because they come in one of the most inflationary periods in modern Canadian economic history.

According to the dominion bureau of statistics the cost of living index is now 150-8 as compared with 100 as the pre-war level. That is indeed a most substantial increase, and one which has occurred largely within the last twelve or fifteen months. In our opinion this will further aggravate the difficulties that many of our people find in meeting the cost of living on the fixed income or salary or wage which they have been receiving for the past number of years. To those people in the more distant parts of Canada who live on such incomes the impact will be the greatest, just as will the impact be the greatest in every respect on those who live farthest away from this part of Canada which we usually describe as central Canada.
The provinces that are most concerned with the export of primary commodities will feel the effect the most. These are the provinces, like my own province of Saskatchewan, where there is very little manufacturing, where they export the bulk of what they produce and where they have to buy nearly all the things they need for the production of that which they export. The same thing applies in parts of British Columbia, in parts of Alberta and Manitoba and in the maritime provinces. These areas are likely to be the most hard hit by the decision of the board.
The freight rates in these regions have always been unusually high in relation to their total production. Into the cost of their production go the costs of the machines and supplies they must purchase, and in the main those costs, as I shall show in a few moments, have to be met by the producer himself. They cannot be passed on to the public.
I wish to point out to the house, and particularly to the government, that a horizontal or across-the-board increase is particularly discriminatory and prejudicial; it does not affect all parts of Canada in the same way and to the same extent. Where, because of competition by water or by road, railway rates are kept down, the 21 per cent increase is obviously less in dollars than it is in regions where the rates are higher because there is not that effective competition. The dollar increases will be larger in British Columbia and in the maritime provinces and on the prairies than they will be in central Canada where this competition does exist.
When we read the story of confederation we realize that this nation as we now know it was largely made possible by the undertaking given at that time by the government and the fathers of confederation that a transcontinental railway line would be built to the Pacific coast, and it was largely on the basis of those bands

Freight Rates
of steel that British Columbia joined confederation. We are linked, then, by those bands of steel, and while the board of transport commissioners could not consider what one may term the political implications in the sense in which I have just noted them, while they apparently felt they had to consider the question purely on the ground of economics, this house and this government are in my opinion obligated to take the wider and the broader view of the conditions under which confederation was established in Canada.
We are linked by those bands of steel. Let us not forget that British Columbians could sell much of their produce and purchase many of their commodities to far greater advantage in the Pacific coast states to the south of the line if those bands of steel ran north and south; that the maritime provinces would benefit enormously through being able to trade with the states on the Atlantic coast of the United States, and that the [DOT] prairie provinces, my own region, would be in a much more advantageous position if the railways ran north and south, thus enabling them to dispose of their goods south of the 49th parallel in Minneapolis and other great cities in the south, and in addition were able to buy their machinery from the United States. But our forefathers decided that we should not link Canada to the United States but build up in this country an independent nation, and we have built up that independent nation along certain lines. One of the bonds that link us together in this country is the bond of railways, those bands of steel to which I have referred. Our forefathers determined to build up an independent Canada, and because of that I submit to the government and to the house that considerations other than those of cold railroad economics must enter into a question of this kind and of this magnitude.
I have said that the substantial increases in ;he rates are bound to make increases necessary in certain price levels. We had a demonstration of that in 1920 when an increase of some 40 per cent was granted to the railways. As I recall the judgment of the board in 1920 I must say that there is one satisfactory feature about the judgment which the board of transport commissioners gave the other day, and that is that there is to be no interference with the Crowsnest rates. We have read the record of the debates of 1920 and recall the controversy that arose then with respect to what are called the Crowsnest rates, and I am glad that we are not faced with that situation again today. But those increases in railway rates were brought about and were followed by a recession, and together they made our whole position, particularly in the
parts of Canada to which I have specifically referred, much more difficult than it might otherwise have been.
I would point out to the house that this judgment of the board is particularly inopportune. Last Saturday the President of the United States signed the European recovery program measure, popularly known as the Marshall plan. We expect that Canada will be called upon to participate in the sending of greater supplies of food and other commodities to Europe under that plan, and of course it will be to our economic advantage to provide those goods. But without effective price controls or subsidies, which have been removed in our country, with an increased demand for our goods without comparable increases in production-and those are not possible to the extent that will be required, because as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) loves to tell us from time to time, we have virtually a condition of full employment now and we cannot increase our productivity to a very large extent - with a greater demand for our goods from without the country and' the maintenance of purchasing power within the country, there is danger of still greater pressure on the price level, and the 21 per cent increase in freight rates authorized by the board of transport commissioners is bound to make that inflationary pressure greater than it otherwise would have been.
We have also to bear in mind that freight rates enter into the price level at many points. They enter into it when the primary commodity which is to be fabricated or processed leaves the farm or other point of origin and goes to the processing point. Secondly, when the fabricated goods leave the processing point and go to the wholesaler, the 21 per cent freight rate increase is again effective, and when the article goes from the wholesaler to the retailer the same thing applies.	Each one of these intermediaries figures his profit on his entire outlay, which includes freight; consequently the increase in freight rates when the commodity reaches the ultimate consumer has been pyramided many times over what it was at the primary point, and the increase in freight rates becomes far more than 21 per cent on that primary article when it ultimately reaches the consumer. And so I say that the freight rate increase will enter into almost every aspect of our price level.
I said a few moments ago that certain competitive carriers exist in certain parts of Canada.	They exist in the province of
Ontario, and when it was announced that
Freight Rates

railway freight rates were to be increased by 21 per cent the truckers met and decided to increase their rates by 15 or 20 per cent- I believe it was 20 per cent-still retaining a competitive position; but because of the increased railway freight rates they are able to increase their own rates very substantially. All this - increased cost of production, the increased cost of living, increased transportation rates-is bound to be reflected in an increased demand for wages. In many lines of work wages in this country are not high. Sometimes it is claimed that the men working on the railways are receiving relatively high wages. But today trains of a hundred cars are operated by the same crew of five as trains of forty cars forty years ago; and so the amount of wages spread over the longer and heavier train is not much more than the wages spread over the smaller train of forty cars.
In any event the demand for increased wages will follow the increased cost of living, and we shall ibe in that inevitable spiral; because wages never catch up with rising prices, and there is unrest when men cannot make both ends meet. Therefore I say that at a time when every effort should be made to reduce living costs and the cost of production, prices will increase and the granting of this increase of 21 per cent to the railroads is a bad example to other industries. We ask other industries to reduce their prices, and at the same time one of the very factors entering into production, the railroads, are permitted a substantial increase in their freight rates. That is why I say it is a bad example to set to other industries.
As usual, in a country like this, freight rates enter into almost every aspect of our commercial relationships. At a time when we need houses for our people, when there is a shortage of dwellings for Canadians, when we need' to ship lumber, cement, steel and other commodities that enter into the building of houses from' one end of the country to the other, we are permitting an increase of 21 per cent on this heavy freight. The result will be more and more difficult in financing the building of houses and in the purchase of homes by those who need them. Altogether the effect, of course, will ultimately be to increase prices and to restrict purchasing power, because when prices rise, individuals have less to spend on things other than their basic needs.
While I do not think there is any immediate prospect of a depression, particularly with the demands that are likely to be made on the Canadian economy in the next year or two, yet we do have a condition of high prices, and inflation inevitably is followed by deflation and depression.

In thinking of the farming community of this country we have to bear in mind that the prices of farm commodities are controlled. As a matter of fact, price ceilings are in effect on several farming commodities, on butter particularly at the present time, and under the new wheat agreement negotiated by the thirty-six countries a ceiling of $2 is set, with a sliding scale downward over the next few years, an agreement which I believe has been made in order to stabilize farm prices, and I think therefore worth while. Nevertheless it has placed a ceiling on the goods the farmer produces, while he will have to meet the increased cost of production that will [DOT] arise because of the increased costs of machines and of the commodities he must buy from outside the areas in which he lives. As a matter of fact that is usually the case with the farmer, because he is one of the producers who cannot pass his costs on to someone else. Usually his prices are pretty well fixed one way or the other, and1 he has to bear any increase in the cost of production, which is unjust.
I said a moment ago-and I want to emphasize it-that the new rates do not affect grain, and I do not want to leave the impression that they do. The price of wheat has been stabilized by an international agreement, and the increased cost of the farmers' machines will have to be borne by himself. May I also say, Mr. Speaker, that at a time when the demands for supplies from North America, and particularly from Canada, are more intense from Europe, naturally there will be an increasing demand for access to the American market, and under the circumstances that is a very legitimate demand. Altogether it seems to me that what this decision has done is to complicate very seriously the situation for Canada, in relation to both our domestic needs and our export demands.
I said the rates are lower in central Canada because of the competitive water and truck haulage. An increase of 21 per cent means less to the people of central Canada than to the people of the maritimes, of British Columbia and of the prairie provinces, but it is still a serious factor in this part of the country, and I do not want to minimize the seriousness of it by the comparison I have just made. The increase of 25 cents a ton in freight on coal, for example, is a serious factor in central Canada, because central Canada is an area which uses vast quantities of coal for industrial purposes and for domestic heating, and every increase in freight always costs much more than the amount of the increase in freight when the commodity reaches the ultimate consumer. Even if the increase is only 25 cents a ton,

Freight Rates
it is bound to be reflected in many ways in central Canada itself. Coal is vital to central Canadian industry; coal is vital in domestic heating in this province and in the neighbouring province where there are no coal deposits.
Apart from these economic considerations the government must consider the political effect of this increase on our regional relationships, to which I have already referred, and ultimately on our international relationships; because if the primary producing areas of Canada are hardest hit and the cost of production increases then their competitive position in world markets is made more difficult. Just at the moment one would not expect that to be a factor, but the day will come when the competitive position of various Canadian primary products will decide the abundance or otherwise of our exports overseas.
A short time ago I read some statistics compiled with regard to the improvements in European farm and productive conditions, and I was particularly struck by the enormous acreage that the Russians seeded last fall in addition to the 1946 fall seedings. I think some seven million additional acres were seeded. Reference was also made to the fact that they are breaking a lot of new land and are going to seed some twenty million acres of fallow land this spring. Bear this in mind: the Russian people accept a much lower standard of living than we do, and the result is that food, which may become a political factor, may also become a matter of economic concern to countries like Canada which experienced the effects of the dumping of cheap wheat on the market back in the early thirties. We should consider how it may affect us again.
Consequently, these freight rates, while grain and so on are excluded, will affect everything that enters into the cost of production of grain. Everything entering into that cost will be affected by the new freight rates which have been authorized by the board of transport commissioners. I say therefore that in view of present world conditions the government should give some consideration to the political implications of the board's judgment. We should endeavour to maintain our associations, both economic and political, with the countries of western Europe and with the United Kingdom, and these associations may depend in no small measure, in a few years' time, upon our ability to sell basic commodities at prices which can be paid by the people overseas and at the same time provide our own people with a reasonable and decent standard of living. But the increase in the freight rates will make it difficult to do either or both of these things.
As I have indicated, the board of transport commissioners could not consider many of the factors I have put before the house this afternoon, but this parliament should and must consider them, and the government should and must do so now. The board, though, admitted that the representations made by some of those who appeared before it were correct. Incidentally, last week the new balance sheet of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company confirmed the statements that were made before the board, that the Canadian Pacific had presented a really pessimistic estimate of its receipts for 1947. Again, that is a factor which the government should take into consideration.
The department of immigration at the present time, from the point of view both of developing our country and, what I think is at the moment even more important, of giving refuge to those who have suffered on account of the war, is bringing to the country many new settlers, some of whom will go into the more remote areas of Canada; and transportation costs will tend, as they have always done, to restrict settlement of those more distant parts.
For example, the district represented by my hon. friend the member for Peace River (Mr. Low) contains enormous quantities of good land yet to be settled. There are various parts of British Columbia, and some parts of Saskatchewan and indeed other sections of our country, which, at a time when we are bringing people into Canada for ultimate settlement, are looking for such settlers; but this freight rate increase will make it more difficult to settle these people economically because of the transportation costs to and from the more remote areas of the things they need or produce.
Then, too, we have to give some attention to the livestock industry. This action will certainly retard expansion in the livestock industry of Canada. It will make hog and dairy production less remunerative because the farmer cannot pass on his increased costs; and already, as has been noted in this house by various hon. members, and admitted by the Minister of Agriculture himself, there has been a serious decline in our hog population in the prairie provinces. At the moment we.are suffering severe shortages in some lines of dairy produce, particularly butter. You can see the consequences of this threatened increase if you consider one or two examples of the effect that will be produced.
I have here a bill for the shipment of thirty-nine head of cattle from a Saskatchewan point to the Toronto market. This Saskatchewan point is near Moose Jaw. It is a little place called Crane Valley. The present
Freight Rates

rate from Crane Valley is $1.09 per 100 pounds. The actual weight of the carload of steers was 21,430 pounds. In the amount I am going to put before the house there was no charge for stopovers and sometimes there are substantial charges for stopovers for various reasons. As I say, the freight charge was $1.09. That amounted to $233.59. Together with the care of the car, and feed en route, the total charge by the railway-and I am advised that it is on that total charge that they can make the increased freight rate- was $238.34. If we take 21 per cent of $238.34, which is the increase to be allowed, we find it amounts to $50.05, which the farmer will have to pay.
It may be said of course that the prices of cattle are relatively high, though they are certainly not as high as they are in the United States, and not as high perhaps as warranted by the present situation, but they are very much higher than I can remember them years ago. I can remember when animals were shipped, not to Toronto from a Saskatchewan point, but to Winnipeg from Saskatchewan points, and the farmers received bills for the freight because the cattle did not pay the freight. In fact, I believe I have such a bill in my files upstairs at the present time. Today of course the prices of cattle compared with those of the time of which I speak are relatively high; and if, as will inevitably happen some time, we have drastic reductions in the price level of these animals, then an increase of $50.05 on a carload of cattle, which is substantial at the present time, will be crippling in the future.
These are factors that should be considered by the government when they are coming to a decision in regard to this matter. Of course, I could give other examples equally striking but I do not propose to weary the house with them. The one I have mentioned will suffice. That one, however, could be multiplied many times in respect of other commodities from the maritime provinces, from British Columbia, and other types of goods from the prairie provinces.
Let me point out that the areas to which I have referred, and particularly perhaps the prairie provinces, have always been penalized by the operations of the tariff policies of various governments. Almost everything we have to buy in order to produce and to live in western Canada has been imported, if not from the United States, with a high tariff, then from eastern Canada, where the manufacturer has taken advantage of the tariff and added on the tariff toll to the cost of his commodity.

speechtext:
We have been penalized by the tariff, and now we are to be penalized by a further increase in freight rates. I should like to suggest that we should not leave the matter there but rather that the government consider an alternative policy. If we are, as we contend, living in a country which has been built up largely upon railway facilities, then the people who live in distant parts of it should not be penalized because they live there. Consideration should be given to the equalization of freight rates across this country, thus recognizing that the railways are indeed a vital factor in the preservation of confederation. If the railways, as is contended, are unable to provide adequate services and to pay proper wages to their staffs with their present revenues, it seems to me that there arises the question of a national transportation policy for this country, that that national transportation policy should be presented to the house by the government, which should take responsibility for recommending it, and that the house should consider it and either modify it or adopt it as the case may be. There should be no regional injustices in order to finance the railways or to keep in operation any part of the Canadian economy. In our opinion an extension of government regulation of competing transportation agencies is overdue. I know that one of the factors in the demand for increased freight rates is that much of the profitable

Freight Rates
freight and passenger traffic is now being carried by buses and trucks. It seems to me that whether the buses or trucks are owned and operated by private companies-and I am not going into that aspect of it this afternoon; let us leave that out-or whether they are operated by governments, we should consider how they can best be integrated into the whole transportation system so that they may feed rather than destroy the great lines of railway upon which this country depends for its existence.
I note that the board of transport commissioners admit that railway freight rates -and I shall be just one minute longer, if I may conclude, Mr. Speaker-should be just and reasonable. I say that they have always been unjust, unreasonable and discriminatory as far as certain parts of this country are concerned, namely, the maritimes, British Columbia, and the prairie provinces. This freight increase makes them more unjustified, more unreasonable and more discriminatory. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to urge upon the government that they take immediate action-not	consideration but	action-to
prevent the increase in rates until a thorough investigation has been made, having regard not only to the economic factors upon which the board delivered judgment but also to the broader political considerations to which I have referred this afternoon, and to present an alternative policy to this house for its consideration.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
It was only to be expected, Mr. Speaker, that the freight rate question would arise in the house after the decision of the board of transport commissioners became known. I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and while I agree with everything he said, I would point out that, as a result of this decision, no province has been harder hit than British Columbia. I can say this also because I am one of the few members in the house who had the responsibility some years ago of appearing before the board of transport commissioners in an appeal with regard to freight rates on grain, and who also had the privilege of appearing before the privy council-which, by the way, is the government -in an appeal against an adverse decision made by the then board of railway commissioners on the same question.
It is not generally recognized-and I am not saying this in a derogatory sense, but rather as a result of experience-that the board of transport commissioners are not doing the job which they were set up to do in the first place. They were set up to protect the public
from the railways; they are now protecting the railways from the public. I say that in all sincerity. This decision which they have made cannot be taken lightly by the government, and I shall make one or two proposals before I sit down. But there are other matters that I want to deal with before making the proposals which I have in mind.
First of all, may I say that I am sorry I came down to the house without my file on freight rates, which I have been keeping since 1934. For sixty years British Columbia has been fighting what is known as the mountain differential in freight rates. They have spent considerable sums of money in appearing before the board of transport commissioners. Here is one thing I found when I appeared before them. It did not matter what argument you placed before the board of transport commissioners, they always came back with this answer: this matter of the differential in freight rates was decided many years ago and we cannot change that decision. The board of transport commissioners are not interested in trade. They are not interested in the development of trade. That is not their job; at least they say it is not their job. But when it comes to an application for an increase of freight rates and passenger fares, this fact should stand out. No real expert from the railways has yet been able to tell the board of transport commissioners just what it costs to haul passengers or to haul a ton of freight. The evidence of the C.P.R. is on record when they had their experts before the board, and not one of them could give the information. It was I believe impossible to tell. Therefore the railways went about their job of putting the charges on the public to the extent, in the words of the old statement, of what the traffic would bear. The differential into British Columbia has been paid for many times over by the people of that province. As was pointed out by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell), when we entered confederation it was understood that we would have a railway on equal terms with the other provinces of Canada. When the C.P.R. went into our province, acting contrary to better judgment and deciding against the route chosen by the government of that day, they picked the highest grade for a railway into the province. We have been victimized right from the beginning, from the time the railway came into the province until the present time. I know that there may be members from Ontario who will get up and say it is wrong for us to contend that we in British Columbia are paying more for freight than they are. But may I point this out to the house. It is strange and significant that in the appeals by the various

Freight Rates
provinces before the board of transport commissioners, Ontario and Quebec were not represented. I ask the people of this country and I ask the government to make inquiries why those two provinces did not appear before the board and make representations.

But in a great national question, when we hear members from the province of Ontario denying that they do not discriminate against other provinces, then certainly it is very strange that on this national question there was no representation, from either Ontario or Quebec.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What is your government doing?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Our provincial government at least has done more than Mr. Drew, because they have already protested. I will wait to hear the protest from Ontario. That at least is something.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I am asking about the government at Ottawa. What are they doing?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We will ask them, too.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You ought to.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I am on my feet now to ask that very question.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But you will not get an answer.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Well I have done more than you; at least I am protesting, while all you are doing is to interrupt. Just let me proceed with my argument. If this is going to be a debate between you and me, then I will accept it. I thought, however, this was above that kind of thing; if it is not, I will abide by any rules you like to put into effect. I believe that before I have finished I shall prove what I say about the benefits received by the two central provinces-especially Ontario-as against British Columbia.
When the, Canadian Pacific railway built into British Columbia they were paid well over $100 million and given, twenty miles of land on each side of the tracks through the province. The people and the government of that day reckoned that we had paid the C.P.R. for coming through the mountains. There still are people who think that when you go to British Columbia you go over the mountains and then drop down. As a matter 
of fact the Canadian National railways has through British Columbia the lowest grade for the whole of Canada. It has a grade of not more than -7 per cent on its low level water route. What does the board of transport commissioners do about the low grade of the C.N.R. as compared with the high grade of the C.P.R.?	The C.N.R. could haul
passengers from Ottawa to British Columbia- Vancouver or New Westminster-twelve hours ahead of the C.P.R.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: More than that.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Well, twelve hours, anyway; I am conservative when I say that.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is good enough.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But are they permitted to do it?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Are they permitted to meet the developments of trucking and transport by air? No, they are not. The board of transport commissioners says: We will not allow the C.N.R. to do it because if you did, it would hurt the C.P.R. Hence I say to the house that the board of transport commissioners is not doing its duty because it is protecting the railways against the best interests of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
They are protecting
private enterprise.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
British Columbia thought it was going to get justice when the Canadian National Railways came into that province. For sixty years we have fought the battle. Before any national increase was allowed in freight rates, the differential to the Pacific coast should have been removed. There should have been equalization before any increase was put into effect.
True, we are getting a kind of sop when g'-ain is left out of the picture-and, although I am not sure of it, I believe coal is also out.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Twenty-five cents a ton.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I know grain is out of it, and I am pleased. But what about all the other commodities? What about the hauling of apples, for instance? What about the rates on the produce we buy in other provinces? As I said, I have not my file with me at the present time, and as a result I have not the latest figures. On other occasions, however,
I have quoted from those records and figures to show that back in 1938, before the war, British Columbia, whilst selling on an export market, bought something like $78,000,000 worth of goods from the two central prov-

Freight Rates
inces, while those two provinces bought goods to the value of $12,500,000 from British Columbia.
In the light of those figures one would think that we would have an equalization of freight rates into British Columbia. But our manufacturers and our other people, when they attempt to ship the same kind of goods back east, have to pay up to 200 per cent more over the same mileage than do the people in the east when they are shipping those products into British Columbia.
I have here one or two newspaper clippings, and while I shall not weary the house by placing all the details on the record ito show the discriminatory rates, I shall mention one or two of them. Let us consider, for instance, items such as bleaching powder and liquid wax, the latter of which comes from Brantford, Ontario. Liquid wax in cans shipped from Brantford to Winnipeg carries a commodity rate of $1.38i per hundred pounds on the all-rail route and $1.28| by the great lakes. On the same goods shipped from Vancouver the rate is not $1.28| but SI .71. Is there any reason why a commodity going east should pay that much more than the same commodity coming west? It is as if a passenger who steps on a train at the Pacific coast were required to pay a higher fare to come to Ottawa than if he were going from Ottawa to the Pacific coast.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: He should pay more to get out there.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
And if any hon. member from Ontario disputes these figures, let him try to correct them if he can. I note in this list mention is made of the town of Chilliwack. From Chilliwack to Winnipeg the rate is S1.26|, whereas if a shipment is made from Sherbrooke to Winnipeg, the same distance, the rate is $1.14. Coffee shipped from Vancouver to Winnipeg would carry a rate of $1.54. whereas if shipped from Montreal to Winnipeg the rate would1 be 96| cents.
One could go on down the list item after item to show this discrimination. It matters little what we have to purchase in British Columbia; the fact is that we have to pay from thirty to two hundred per cent more on the goods we buy from Ontario and Quebec than we should be called upon to pay.
There is something else entering into the picture of freight rates which is not generally understood, and that is that sometimes rates are made in the United States. There is in existence an organization known as the Canadian Freight Association, with headquarters in Chicago. In 1941 one of the local manufacturers in Vancouver wanted to manufacture an article in that city and ship it to eastern Canada. But strange as it may seem, when an appeal was placed before the Canadian Freight Association, which, I understand, is an association of railway interests of Canada and the United States, an adverse decision was given. This association meets and decides rates. The rate was decided by the Canadian Freight Association in the city of Chicago. Representatives of the two countries meet and I suppose they see to it that the .Canadian rate does not go too low in case it might draw traffic away from the United States. It is a serious matter for the people' of this country, especially at a time like this when they are called upon to pay an increase of 21 per cent over what they have been paying.
I know the railways are having difficult times these days, but I think this is partly due to the antiquated system under which they are operating. I may be wrong, but I know that if one travels on the Great Northern Railway he may leave the city of Vancouver and be in Toronto almost one day sooner than he would if he travelled by either of the Canadian lines. That railway is operating so efficiently that it is meeting the competition of air travel, and the cost is no greater. This is a condition to which we should give serious thought.
I want to repeat-because I think it should be said again-that the Canadian National Railways have been held down by the Canadian Pacific both in the matter of freights and in the matter of passengers. I do not know particularly about the prairie provinces, but I do know that in and out of British Columbia the Canadian National Railways can haul two to three times the passenger or freight cars hauled by the Canadian Pacific, owing to the fact that on the C.P.R. there is at some points a grade of 2-5 per cent whereas on the C.N.R. they have a low level water route stretching right from the coast to the prairies of not over -7 per cent.
On a number of occasions I have informed the British Columbia government that it is useless to appeal to the board of transport commissioners for a reversal of their judgments. Therefore we must come to the real appeal board, to the foot of the throne, to the crown, in order to present our case. I am pleading as hard as I can and as sincerely as I can that the government do not allow this increase to be put into effect until the whole matter of freight rates is reviewed by some body other than the board of transport commissioners. The board of transport commissioners are so hedged in with past decisions they have made that you might just as well
Freight Rates

stay home. Unless you want to see the capital city of Ottawa you will be just wasting time and money to come down here.
I think I mentioned a little while ago that the Canadian Pacific had obtained an additional concession in British Columbia through being granted an injunction against the operation of trucks in the national parks. Truck transportation in the national parks has therefore been eliminated, and the people in the interior are still called upon to pay high freight rates with the mountain differential, whereas if this injunction had not been granted freight by trucks could be operated to the prairie provinces.
I could mention many cases, but I shall refer to only one or two to show how their decisions and their attitude have restricted trade. A few years ago a certain manufacturer wanted the right to operate his trucks in bond from Vancouver to Calgary. As hon. members know, there is no national highway through to the prairie. He had a contract to deliver five tons of fresh fish which he was going to freight from Vancouver to Calgary. He told me that he could land that fish in Calgary three hours ahead of the railway express and then bring back to the province grain which he could carry at rates cheaper than those charged by the railways. But they would not allow him to send his trucks through in bond.
I say without fear of successful contradiction that our whole attitude to railway freight rates and to the railways is wrong. Many hon. members have advocated the construction of a highway from one end of the country to the other, and in my opinion the reason we do not have such a highway is that the railways fear it and have blocked progress. Something has to be done.
I know that losses by the railways have to be taken care of, but it is also a fact that there is much duplication of railway lines. I think it was the late Sir Edward Beatty who said that at least $60,000,000 to $75,000,000 could be saved if the railroads could get together to eliminate the duplication of lines in certain districts. It might well be under a new set-up they could haul all the freight into British Columbia over the Canadian National and all passengers over the Canadian Pacific. I am not sure, but I feel quite certain that if we had only the Canadian National running into British Columbia we would not be paying the high rates we are called upon to pay today.
I am going to conclude my remarks by strongly appealing to the government, and in all sincerity, to step in on behalf of the people of Canada and not permit this decision to be

put into effect. I submit that the whole freight rate structure of Canada, particularly that of British Columbia, is antiquated and out of date under modern conditions. It is just something which has been set up to make the public pay.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What the traffic will bear.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: All the traffic will bear, as one hon. member s^ys. I think that expresses it very well. I appeal to the government to consider this decision seriously in the light of what we consider to be the needs of the present situation.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this debate until I listened to hon. members attacking the provinces of Ontario and Quebec with regard to the decision on freight rates. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec have nothing to do with freight rates; those rates are set by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. If those two provinces saw fit not to appear before the transport board with regard to freight rates, that was their own business. The other seven provinces did appear and tens of thousands of dollars were spent by governments on experts and legal counsel in order that the case might be placed before the transport board. This having been done, the board finally rendered a decision.
I listened attentively this afternoon to the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell). I was not sure as he went along whether he was or was not opposed to the increase.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That was obvious.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Just wait until I am through. I was not sure whether he was opposed to the increase, but as he concluded his speech I realized that he was opposed to it. What is the actual situation? Like any other business or industry in this country, no matter how small or how large, the railways were faced with increased costs during the war and it was impossible for them to renovate their roadbeds and cars and other equipment. They have to do that now. Anyone who travels on the railways knows very well how much they are in need of new equipment. I think every Canadian will say that no transportation system in the world did a.better job during the war than our railways. They carried on with only one major disaster during those years.
The board has made its decision. Differentials in freight rates are a matter of government policy; they are something for the government itself to decide. If the government is prepared to pay subsidies, or whatever you may call it, on freight moving east or west

Freight Rates
from the central provinces, that is a matter of government policy. Surely we should not condemn the railroads or the board of transport commissioners because of the decision that has been made.
I thought that after the motion had been made this afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) or some other responsible minister of the crown would have made a statement as to the government policy with respect to this decision. So far we have not heard that.
The hon. member who has just sat down made a speech taking to task the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec and telling us of the sorry plight of British Columbia in the matter of freight rates. We heard cheers from the members from the maritimes and the western provinces when the leader of the C.C.F. was speaking. I wonder why they did not bring to bear upon the government itself some of the arguments which they use in this house and ask the government to see to it that a policy is adopted which will bring freight rates more into line with national conditions.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Because we are outnumbered.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My hon. friend says
"because we are outnumbered". It seems peculiar that a group of men representing the west and the maritimes in this house have not sufficient influence within their own party to get it to adopt a policy that is good for the whole nation. Nevertheless that is the situation.
Under the Railway Act there is an appeal against the rates where discrimination can be shown.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Then what happens?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I have found some very favourable decisions given even where rail and water transport competed'. In the summer months, when we had water transportation on the inland lakes, I have found the board favourably inclined to seeing that moderate rates were set, even when there was no competition from the railways. My hon. friend said that if only the Canadian National ran to British Columbia the situation would be different altogether. Surely he realizes that where you have competition you have lower rates. In all my experience, and I have had considerable experience with railways and steamship companies, I have found that where only one line runs into a town or village the rate is higher because there is no competition. My hon. friend must mean by his argument that if the National line ran into British Columbia it would see to it that it got-

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We would have had that, but the board of transport commissioners would not grant it.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Let me say that the board of transport commissioners is a creature of the government which my hon. friend supports, and if there is dissatisfaction with the board there is only one thing for the government to do.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the board of transport commissioners is not a creature of the government, as my hon. friend knows, but a creature of parliament, which is an entirely different thing. While I am on my feet perhaps he will allow me to say, as I did not want to interrupt him when he referred to government policy concerning equalization, that under the Railway Act equalization of tolls and facilities is a matter for the board of transport commissioners to decide. I am not denying the responsibility of the government upon appeal, but I say to my hon. friend that that is the situation under the act.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I appreciate what my hon. friend says, but he might as well say that the budget itself is a creature of parliament; nevertheless it embodies the policy of the government. If I were sitting on the government benches and had any authority, and if the board of transport commissioners in my opinion were not acting in the general welfare of this country, I would fire them and appoint a board that would so act, and my hon. friend knows that only too well.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I know no such thing.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is all very well to say that the board is a creature of parliament, but if this government wanted to change the board tomorrow and brought in a bill for the purpose, every member of the house knows that it would go through and there would be a new board.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And who would object to that more than my hon. friend?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Certainly I would. But if I were on the government side I would not. Let us be frank about these things. If I were sitting with the government I would certainly see that the policies I believed in were carried out, and if the board of transport commissioners were not carrying out the policy of the government, I would change the board. Let the government bring in a policy that will satisfy every member from the east and from the west.
I listened very carefully to the leader of the C.C.F. this afternoon and I heard his
Freight Rates

reference to buses and trucks. I was in the Ontario legislature for a number of years at a time when motor vehicle traffic was starting to build up in this province from 173,000 licences until today there are some 1,200,000 licences in the province. At that time the railways were dead to the issue. They were not paying much attention to the bus and truck competition, but finally they realized it was a factor. The leader of the C.C.F. said that we should work out a transportation policy in this country that would integrate the bus and truck traffic with the railways. In other words it was a mild way of saying that we should nationalize or socialize the whole bus, truck and railway business in this country. That of course would be their policy if they came into power.
I believe that the question of the differential and the question of the equalization of freight rates must be the responsibility of the government, and the government must accept that responsibility. I do not see how the government can go against the board of transport commissioners which has said that there must be a 21 per cent increase in freight rates. I do not see how the government can say to the railways: You are not going to have that increase. The question has been under investigation for over a year. The greatest legal minds in the country appeared before the board for the railways, and against them were arrayed the best legal minds the government could get to refute their arguments. Having heard the evidence and the argument the board decided that there must be a 21 per cent increase in freight rates. In view of that fact I do not see how the government can say to the railways: You are not going to have that increase. But, on the other hand, if the government as a result of this increase decides that there must be a new policy of equalization if there is discrimination as between the east and west and the central provinces, that is a matter of government policy.
This afternoon the leader of the C.C.F. put his party on record as being opposed to increased freight rates. He said that the railways were the bond that bound together the provinces of this dominion. That might have been the case at one time, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Why not now?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Certain promises were
made at confederation to provide railway communication between the provinces, and that was done. But we have grown up since then, and today there are much stronger bonds than those bands of steel of which the leader of the C.C.F. spoke. They are the bonds of Canadian nationhood, which have

been welded time and time again in the last thirty years, when men and women from every province banded together and went out to fight for the safety of this country. Those are much stronger than bands of steel to bind this country together. I would hate to think that it was only because of economic conditions that we as provinces were banded together into one nation.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Not on this issue.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I come from the province of Ontario and I believe that to build up a nation we must be prepared to give and take. There cannot be any east and there cannot be any west; there cannot be any Quebec and there cannot be any Ontario. We have to be willing to give and take, to give more and take less. If we all adopt that attitude we will get along much better.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Why do you not practise it?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I say to my hon. friend that I have practised it all my political life, which is more than my political friend can say.
This afternoon the leader of the C.C.F. party rose in his place and condemned the increase in freight rates. I remember an occasion some three or four years ago when a few of us, members of all parties in the house, were gathered together. A by-election had been held that day. It looked as though the C.C.F. candidate might be elected, -but he was defeated. On the same day a labour organization met in the city of Montreal and passed a resolution stating that they would endorse the C.C.F. as the political arm of labour. A certain C.C.F. member who was sitting with the group said, "Well, we lost the by-election, but look at the tremendous victory we have won. We now have the C.C.L. and the C.I.O. unions of this country adopting the C.C.F. as the political arm of labour." All down through the last few years we have found1 that the heads of the C.I.O. and the C.C.L. unions have come out and tried to turn the members of their unions into a political field that is foreign to most of them. They have tried to make them vote for C.C.F. candidates. They are forgetting all their trade union principles and are paying more attention to the political arm of labour than to the injustices under which the trade union members may be suffering. Today the political arm of the C.I.O. and the C.C.L. is more important to the leaders of these organizations than fighting for the rights of the men who belong to the unions. Today in this house we have the leader of the C.C.F. party condemning the increase in freight rates, and' his great political pal, who he hopes will be able to send

Freight Rates
many more C.C.F. members to the House of Commons and' to the various legislatures of Canada, Mr. Mosher, says that the increase in rates is not enough; that it should be a great deal more. I realize that politics makes strange bedfellows, but" this combination is about the strangest that I have ever seen. It was surprising to me today to bear the leader of the C.C.F. party condemn the decision of the board1 of transport commissioners at a time when the men who form a great part of the labour unions, and whom the leaders are trying to have pledge their support to the C.C.F., are demanding higher wages and are saying that the only way they can get them is to have the railways increase their earnings.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are in this position. The board of transport commissioners have made a decision. The decision has been made as the result of careful consideration on their part and, I would say, as the result of the argument of the best legal minds in this country and the advice of the best chartered accountants. The case was ably presented to the board of transport commissioners. If the decision of the board means discrimination, if it means unfairness in rates, then it comes back on the lap of the government, and the government must accept the responsibility of bringing down such a policy as will rectify any discriminations there may be. Let us deal with this thing not from a political angle but in a realistic way. Let us realize that our two great railways are two of the most important parts of our whole economy. They have done a wonderful job down through the years, and will do a greater job in the future. Surely we should not stand in this house and condemn them today. Rather we should condemn the lack of policy of the government, if there is such a thing as discrimination, as some of my hon. friends opposite from the east and the west have said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31

speechtext: Yes.

My hon. friend was
correct when he said that the leader of this group opposed this increase. Will the hon. member state whether he is in favour of or opposed to the 21 per cent increase?

speechtext: I will say this to my hon. friend, and I have always maintained the same policy. No industry, no business in this country, can adequately pay its employees what they should get unless it has the earnings with which to do it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Is the answer yes or no?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Have you stopped beating your wife?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Apparently you have not.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: In closing I say this-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Without an answer.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I appeal to the government to handle this matter in such a way that we can face the future with a reasonable assurance that there will be no discrimination as between various parts of the country. I appeal to the government to give us a railway policy which will help build up this country as we hope to see it built up.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking for this group in the house on March 10, 1947, as recorded at page 1229 of Hansard, I said that in the matter of freight rates the Social Creditors stated their position clearly in the Alberta brief on dominion-provincial relations entitled "The case for Alberta," published in 1938. I pointed out at that time that in view of the existing discrimination in the freight rate structure against the western provinces, and particularly against the province of Alberta, we advocated a downward revision of freight rate structure for western Canada rather than any increase. I also said that we realized the fact that it was in the best interests of Canada to have an efficient and smooth running railway service; and if it could be shown that the railways need additional revenue to operate efficiently we would not oppose any justifiable adjustment, but definitely not at the expense of the prairie provinces or of any other one section of Canada. I can only emphasize the point that the load should be borne equally by the entire nation; but to determine the financial position of the railways the house should be supplied with accurate figures as to the earnings and operating costs of the railways in order that the members may be in a position to consider this question intelligently. Failing this, Social Crediters have no other choice than to oppose any upward revision of freight rates and to continue pressing for a downward revision of freight rates for the prairie provinces, and for a fair equalization of freight rates for the entire country.
I do not intend to argue at this time the effect which the increase in freight-cost will have on the cost of living in Canada. Suffice it to say that $70,000,000 additional freight-cost will be imposed on the Canadian people in addition to the already high cost of living in this country.
Freight Rates

I notice that the spokesmen for the railway companies have stated that they will perhaps need and ask for further increases as time goes by, and several of them have asked what would happen if the railways were to go bankrupt. I do not think any reasonable, responsible Canadian would want to see our railways bankrupt. We believe that, should the railways require additional revenue, they should have it. But as I have pointed out. we cannot support discrimination such as has been practised in the past.
In the Montreal Gazette of April 1, 1948. there appeared an editorial which placed before, the Canadian people views which in my opinion should be corrected. The editorial stated:
One of the most important features of this week's judgment of the transport board on railway freight rates was that it upheld the railways' insistence on an inclusive, uniform percentage increase applying equally to all areas of the country and all rates embraced by the decision. Both by inference and by stated conclusions, the judgment unequivocally rejected the vehement, often stormy demands for special favours that would lift or reduce the burden of any increase for the prairie province and the maritimes. The board is to be commended for thus firmly resisting the considerable pressures, political and otherwise, brought to bear upon it to discriminate between different geographic regions and economic categories of the country as a whole. The award upholds the sound principle that the rate increases finally found necessary shall be spread evenly across the general rate structure and borne pro rata by all classes and areas of the national community.
That statement is an interesting one but it is totally misleading. Let me quote two sentences from an article written by the Hon. Stuart Garson, Premier of Manitoba, which appeared in the Edmonton Journal on November 22, 1947:
In the current freight rates hearings before the transport board of Canada, exhibit 131 filed by the Canadian Pacific Railway, shows that in the ten years from 1936 to 1945 inclusive, 65-8 per cent of the operating profits of the Canadian Pacific Railway were made in western Canada. Unfortunately, no comparable figures are available from the Canadian National Railways.
In the light of that statement, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is there no discrimination, as the Montreal Gazette states? Not only that, but let me point out something else. The population of Canada in 1941 was 11,506,655. The western provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba had a population of 3,239,766, and the rest of Canada, the larger part of Canada, or what we in the western provinces usually call eastern Canada, had a population of 8,266,889.
Now 3,239,766 people in the four western provinces contributed to the profit of the

Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in the ten years mentioned by Mr. Garson, 65-8 per cent, while 8,266,889 people contributed, in the same ten year period, only 34-2 per cent of the operating profit of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is the point; that is the pivot on which our argument is based. I want to repeat it because it is the strongest argument and one which cannot be refuted, an argument which totally disproves any contention that western Canada is not being discriminated against-and, of course, the maritime provinces. The fact that 3,239,766 people contribute 65-8 per cent to the operating profit of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, while 8,266,889 people contribute only 34-2 per cent is an argument that cannot be brushed aside. Let someone answer it.
Let me point out further that the standard rate for first-class freight east of Fort William and Port Arthur is fifty-eight cents for 100 pounds for 100 miles. West of Fort William the first-class rate is sixty-five cents for the same weight and distance. Moreover, discrimination is also practised in applying the process known as "tapering", by which standard rates per mile are reduced on long hauls. On a 500 mile haul in the eastern division this reduction amounts to 25 per cent on the mileage rate for short hauls, while in the west the reduction is only 11-4 per cent; yet long hauls are more common in western Canada than in eastern Canada.
Here are some other important and striking examples of discrimination. Take lumber. A carload of lumber shipped from a. Quebec lumber centre, Mont Laurier to Glencoe, Ontario, a distance of 643 miles, pays twenty-three cents per 100 pounds. On the other hand, a carload shipped from Vancouver to Calgary, also a distance of 643 miles, pays fifty cents per hundredweight. Again, let us take freight charges from Okanagan Landing to Calgary, a distance of 358 miles. The cost is $1.04 per hundredweight, while for practically the same distance, from Hamilton to Vaudreuil, 355 miles, the cost is sixty-five cents per hundredweight. Then from Okanagan Landing to Red Deer, 453 miles, the rate is $1.41 per hundredweight, and from Hamilton to Isbister, a distance of 453 miles, the rate is 91^ cents per hundredweight.
On a carload of domestic grain the rate per 100 miles is 7i cents per hundredweight in the east, fifteen cents on the prairies and seventeen cents in British Columbia. Then again it costs forty-nine cents per hundredweight to ship grain from Streamstown, Alberta, to Vancouver, a distance of 995 miles; while it

Freight Rates
costs only twenty cents to ship it from Fort William to Montreal exactly the same distance.
Let me give one or two other examples. A carload of flannelette blankets intended for Vancouver may be sent under a special "cotton goods" rate of $1.75 per hundredweight. A similar carload sent to Edmonton is put in an entirely different classification at $4,531 per hundredweight.

Some of these examples I have cited are absolute proof that our freight rate structure as it has existed for many years is out of date and, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has stated, should be overhauled. I want to point out that the board of transport commissioners sat on this case for 174 sitting days. If the decision which they handed down is the best they could do in 174 sitting days, I do not know what they would hatch if they continued sitting much longer. We must realize that the time has arrived for Canada to organize her freight rate structure on a sound, scientific basis. This discrimination which has been practised for so long, by placing as much burden on the western provinces as they can possibly bear, has run its limit. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that members and the people in western Canada are not against the central provinces. We are not blaming the central provinces, but we certainly place the responsibility for the freight structure on the doorstep of the government.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) mentioned that the board of transport commissioners was named or set up by this parliament. That is true. But it is also true that the government has the power to overrule any decision of the board; the minister knows that. Surely the time has come for us to realize that the people in western Canada should not be asked to continue bearing the burden they bore during the thirties and of course, since then, with regard to freight rates. Why should three million people pay into the treasury of the railway company by way of freight rates twice as much as eight million pay? There is no justifiable reason for it.
It is pointed out in the press that because the C.P.R. had a deficit of $33,737 for the
month of February, the position of the C.P.R. was shaky and therefore western Canada and the maritimes must stand the burden. Let me say this. If I know the people of western Canada at all, this time it will not be sufficient for hon. members to rise in their places and speak for fifteen or twenty minutes or forty minutes and then mail out a number of copies of Hansard to their key men and say, "You see, we tried our best, but the government did not do anything about it; they let the board of transport commissioners put it through." That will not be enough this time. My view is that any member from the three western provinces, regardless of the party he represents, or from the maritimes-

The hon. member for
Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) stated that the railways needed money to replace their equipment. He also pointed out that the railways rendered a great service to Canada during the war years. That is all true. I do not think anyone in a reasonable frame of mind would deny that. But that does not mean that we in western Canada should have to fork out some more cash to contribute an even greater proportion than before in order to help out the railways. I feel that, as I have already pointed out, the time has come for this government to find ways and means of arriving at some scientific solution to this problem. Surely it is not fair for us to carry this burden any longer.
I notice some headings in papers published in western Canada, and I just want to make a brief reference to this. One of them goes on to say, "West provinces get concession." How do you like that? Then they go on to say, "The prairie provinces received a substantial concession in Tuesday's freight rate judgment." A substantial concession!
Another newspaper goes on to state:
Western farmers naturally will be pleased with the concession on western grain movements made by the board of transport commissioners . . .
It is almost tragic. Why make or print statements of that sort when -we know that the primary producer-that is, the farmer-is the
Freight Rates

only one who pays freight on the things he buys and on the things he sells? He pays double, and he is the only one who does that. If hon. members try to find examples of this in the secondary industries, they will not be able to do so. Those industries do not pay freight both ways; not at all. But the farmer must pay it. Then the headlines are put in the paper-to mislead the farmer, to leave that sweet taste with him after he has been given a pill of the rise of 21 per cent in freight rates -that the farmer "has been granted a concession." I say, let us be fair and let us be grown up. I would appeal to hon. members on all sides of the house to take this matter under consideration and solve the problem properly.
I do not object to the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) bringing this matter to the attention of the house this afternoon. I feel, however, that a question of this kind requires more study on the part of members wishing to take part in debate. Judging from the debate thus far, I would conclude that other members and the leader of the C.C.F. have spoken more effectively on other subjects. Hon. members on all sides of the house would have gained much had they known this matter was to be discussed today, and had they had an opportunity to prepare the material they wished to place before parliament and to place it on Hansard, so that the people might read what was said and learn something more about this question.
