Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat when he states things are moving so rapidly today that it is difficult for hon. members or the public generally to follow what is taking place. We have got away from the horse-and-buggy stage and are trying to develop a streamlined society. Therefore we have to keep on our toes all the time; that is all there is to it.
However, the subject matter before us this afternoon is not new. The fact of the matter is that freight rates have been discussed in the press for the last two or three years, and we have been told repeatedly that the railways were seeking an increase of 30 per cent in freight rates. I think no apology is necessary for having introduced the subject this afternoon. My recollection is that before the Easter adjournment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that the first order of business would be the discussion of a bill to subsidize gold production. I believe the discussion this afternoon is much more to the point than would be a discussion having for its purpose the subsidizing of a metal dug in Canada and buried in the United States. Surely this discussion is more timely.
I should like to say only a few words for the benefit of the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). I know what I shall say is out of order, but no more so than what he said. The hon. member was allowed to place his observations on record and to accuse the leader of the C.C.F. of being more interested in the Canadian Congress of Labour and the C.I.O. than in matters affecting the people generally.
Just for a start, let me point out to the hon. member that there is in Canada no such organization as the C.I.O. It is an American organization which has in the Canadian Congress of Labour its counterpart in Canada. It is not a union; rather it is a body having for its purpose the co-ordinating of industrial unionists in Canada and the United States, and the handling of their legislative problems. After many years of experience of going cap in hand to governments, unions very wisely decided that it was about time to send some of their own men into the lawmaking bodies so that they might help to make laws which might be in keeping with their own ideas. And so, just as the manufacturers' association, the chambers of commerce, the National Steel Company of Canada, DOSCO and others have

Freight Rates
selected Liberal and Tory parties as their political agents-and contribute to their campaign funds-so the labouring men of Canada, through that industrial organization, in convention and after discussion, decided that they, too, would select a political party.
The hon. member for Waterloo South does not like that; but let me tell him that the selection was made without any solicitation on our part. He tried to show conflict between the statement by Mr. Mosher, head of the Canadian Congress of Labour, to the effect that the increase in freight rates was not great enough, and the statement by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in the house that an increase in freight rates at this time was unwarranted.
Surely that should not surprise the hon. member for Waterloo South. I understand that at one time he sat as a labour member in the Ontario legislature. He should know that Mr. Mosher, as head of the railway unions, is the sales agent of the labourers and employees of Canadian railways. As such it is his job to sell that labour power at the highest possible figure. And in this House of Commons the leader of the C.C.F., as leader of a socialist party in Canada the objective of which is a new order of society in this country, is doing his job to fight for the changes in the mechanics of society which would make it unnecessary to do those things such as we are now doing under this present scheme of increasing freight rates.

And I want to pass this into the ears of my Tory friends, that so long as the mechanics of society are as they are today this is the procedure which will have to be taken. It cannot be done in any other way than it is being done today, so long as you stick to this capitalist system of so-called free enterprise. And what you are ranting and raving against today in the light of this increased schedule of freight rates, and the hardship it will create among people throughout Canada, is the very thing for which the people of this country voted when they voted to retain a system of free enterprise, represented by either Liberal or Tory candidates. They are getting what they asked for.
Let me say a further word about communism-because the hon. member also injected that into the debate. I do not care whether it is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) or the hon. member for Waterloo South who rises in his place in the house
anil tries to create the impression that the democratic socialist party of Canada is exactly the same as the communist party of Russia; if either does it, then he is doing this country a great disservice.

And he is doing exactly what was done in Europe. He sowed seeds of suspicion and confusion, until such time as that Mr. Bolsheviki he is so afraid of came in and took things over, because they arose out of the confusion created by men who should have had better sense.
Let me say further to the hon. member for Waterloo South that the only countries in Europe which stood up to Hitler and which have not capitulated to this totalitarian machine of Russia are the countries where there were well developed social democratic parties based upon trade unions and cooperatives.

The people there were welded together politically and economically, and there was no vacuum into which that machine could creep so as to destroy the structure of society. Those Scandinavian countries stood up, as did Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia. And if that development does not take place in this country, despite all this talk about democracy-at least the way it has been talked about from those sources to whom I am directing this little bit of advice- you are apt to wind up behind the eight ball and get the very sort of thing you are afraid of.
Let us get back to this business of freight rates and the Canadian National Railways. My contention is that there are two pertinent points in connection with this whole matter that should be made clear. In so far as the maritimes are concerned I believe that this increase of 21 per cent across the board has destroyed the effect of the Maritime Freight Rates Act.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, but I have in my hand the judgment rendered by the board of transport commissioners in the application of the railway association of Canada on behalf of its member railway companies for authority to make a general increase in tolls and freight rates. I have read this over, and I am going to call the attention of the minister to a part that strikes me particularly, to be found on page
Freight Rates

69. This deals with the Maritime Freight Rates Act and it quotes section 8 of the act which reads:
The purpose of this act is to give certain statutory advantages in rates to persons and industries in the three provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward island, and in addition upon the lines in the province of Quebec mentioned in section two, together hereinafter called "select territory," accordingly the board shall not approve nor allow any tariffs which may destroy or prejudicially affect such advantages in favour of persons or industries located elsewhere than in such select territory.
When I read that over I came to the conclusion that that practically wipes out any advantage the maritiines may have because of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and others have stated that neither the province of Quebec nor the province of Ontario was represented at this hearing because they were not interested. My impression is that the 21 per cent increase in freight rates which will be applied both east and west will not be applied in central Canada, because the competition from trucking companies is so great and the hauls so short in those provinces that if the increase is applied it will simply mean driving business to the trucking companies. I hear a rumour to the effect that the trucking companies are going to jack up their rates by 20 per cent but I do not know how true it is.
In view of the fact that our principal exports are coal and steel, this increase imposes an additional burden in marketing our products in central Canada. I shall go into this further later on. In addition, a large percentage of what we eat and wear in eastern Canada comes from the central provinces. We did have some advantages under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, but in my reading of that small section of the report those advantages are wiped out. I think that is also the opinion of the maritime transportation commission as set out in their representations to the government.

Secondly, I do not believe that this board had any authority or right to proceed with this hearing or to make that report, and I shall read from the report in order to justify my contention. The board of transport commissioners merely acted in this matter as the agents of the railroads. I quote from page 70 as follows:
Mr. Burehell, one of the counsel for the maritime provinces, contended that the applicant railways had failed to adduce any evidence to show that there has been an increase in the cost of railway operation in Canada between the first day of July, 1927, and the present time and that the board was, therefore, without jurisdiction or authority to permit any increase in freight rates which would include the "select territory" until satisfactory evidence has been furnished of such increased cost. And that this omission on the part of the applicants could only be remedied by a further substantive application on their part for the purpose, and upon due notice to the respondents.
Mr. Cross, a member of the board said:
I must agree with the argument of counsel for the maritimes that the applicants, it may be through inadvertence, did not furnish us with specific evidence, or in any event sufficient evidence, of increased cost of railway operation in Canada over the cost prevailing on July the first, 1927.
According to this report, the board of transport commissioners went ahead and appointed Mr. John C. Lessard-

To require the applicant railways to proceed by way of substantive application, as suggested by counsel for the maritimes. would involve much delay in disposing of the most important question before us. This further delay should, 1 think, be avoided if it can be fairly done.
The board has, I think, power to investigate and ascertain the facts itself and to make a finding based upon the results of such investigation, and we have proceeded accordingly.
The board instructed Mr. John C. Lessard, its then director of the bureau of transportation economics, to investigate and ascertain the facts, as to whether the cost of railway operation in Canada has increased since July 1, 1927, and if so, to what extent, and to report thereon to the board. These instructions were carried out and Mr. Lessard reported to the board.
My contention is that, in view of the fact that the Canadian National Railways had been contending for at least two or three years that they required an increase in rates, it was reasonable to expect that they would have had their case prepared and in the hands of the board of transport commissioners rather

than the board setting themselves up as a body to investigate the costs of the Canadian National Railways. The board sent in one man and upon that one man's evidence they permit an increase of 21 per cent in the freight rates across this country.
I think it was an absolutely stupid thing to do. I do not think the board of transport commissioners had any right to set themselves up as the agents of the Canadian National Railways in order to gather evidence which should have been placed in their hands by an organization which in my opinion has sufficient economic divisions, research facilities and all that kind of thing to have prepared a report to be placed in the hands of the board.

This thing was done absolutely wrongly, and it is a serious matter for the people of this country.
Where does the question of provincial rights come in? I understand that seven provinces are opposed to this increase in freight rates. I know that three maritime provinces, working through the maritime transportation commission, have made or are making representations to the government asking for a stay of execution, and I mean execution literally, because this increase is execution so far as the maritime provinces are concerned. It is the final kick in the face for these displaced provinces which will put them on their back. Seven provinces I understand, apart from Ontario and Quebec, have made or are making representations to the government asking that the application of th;s judgment be withheld for at least thirty days to give them a chance to appeal. I understand that the rates become operative on April 8. Let us take a look at this question of appeal. In order to appeal you must first get permission from the board of transport commissioners-

-or you must get the permission of the supreme court itself. Far be it from me to suggest that the board could influence the judiciary of this country. I will not suggest that at all, nor would I suggest that the judiciary might in some cases be political appointees. I think the cards are stacked against the people of this country getting redress along the lines of an appeal. I would ask the minister when he replies to tell the house if he or the cabinet intend to consider the matter of withholding the application of these new rates for at least thirty days in order to give the seven provinces who are dissatisfied with the judgment the opportunity of making an appeal.
What does this increase in freight rates mean to the cost of living? In the maritime provinces it means a lot more than the average member here realizes. For instance, to start with, there is a flat increase of twenty-five cents a ton on coal, whether on long or short hauls. In reality that amounts to a flat increase of fifty cents a ton on most of the coal of the maritime provinces. Take the coal shipped over the Sydney and Louisburg railway. That is a company-owned road, and it comes under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The company will haul coal from Sydney to Louisburg or from Glace Bay to Sydney and there is a twenty-five cent increase per ton on coal going that distance. Then the coal is transferred to the Canadian National Railways, where an additional twenty-five cents a ton has to be paid. So on practically 85 per cent of the production of coal in the maritime province? there is a flat increase, not of twenty-five cents, but of fifty cents a ton. In Cumberland county, on the Cumberland railway, and on the Sydney and Louisburg railway-and most of the coal is produced in this area-the two rates will apply. I notice that Mr. Ralston, one of the counsel for the maritimes, made a very strong argument on this point; but all the satisfaction he got, according to the report, was: Oh, there are incidentals like that which will have to be taken care of as we go along. But in the meantime the rates are applied, and once they are applied they have the habit of sticking. The time to cure the thing is before the rates are applied. But even assuming that the increased rate was only twenty-five cents a ton on coal, if the minister acquiesces, if he agrees with the board's judgment-

speechtext:
What I am trying to do is to have the minister prepare some pretty good notes so that he will be in a position to make a clear and definite statement to the house when he speaks. I am trying to draw information out of him. I want to know what the cabinet thinks about this thing, because the cabinet is now the only body with power to prevent this rate from becoming operative pending a hearing before the courts of the country. That is why I am addressing the minister. He presides over the department that has jurisdiction over the board; he is a member of the cabinet, and if we can make him see how serious this thing is the chances are that he will appeal to his colleagues from Ontario and Quebec and say: The maritimes have got a bad kicking around already and this increase is a bad kick in the nose to them, so perhaps we had better let up and stagger this thing, transfer some portion of the burden to the central part of the country.
The minister will agree that the maritime transportation commission is headed by capable people. I do not think anyone would consider that body as being political in any way, shape or form. It represents some seventy boards of trade. I have met some of them. I do not know what their politics are and I do not care. I have always believed that they were interested in the part of the country in which they live and that they were continually trying to improve conditions there. They feel very strongly about this increase. Here is a long press statement giving the views of the commission. I presume the minister has read it. I shall not take time to read it, but it points out that this freight increase will add to the cost of living tremendously because there are sections of Nova Scotia where 80 per cent of what the people eat is imported, dragged all the way from the central part of Canada, and this additional freight rate will not only add to the cost of living but hamper the marketing of Nova Scotia's basic materials. The only things we send out of the province are steel to be fabricated, and our coal, which we are trying to get back into the Quebec market which we lost during the war.

As I said, the maritime transportation commission feel very strongly about this increase and they have written much stronger stuff in the press than what I am saying here this afternoon. They say also that the increase in the freight rates, rather than encouraging subsidiary industry which is so badly needed in the maritimes, will back it further and further away. It means a continuation of unemployment; perhaps it means creating more unemployment. The last government figures showed that today 27,000 people are unemployed in the maritimes, and there is not a chance in the world for them to get a job. There was some work for them under the displaced persons program which the federal government operated. Under that program they assisted the people from the maritimes to go to central Canada. Today they have been displaced by the displaced persons whom the government is bringing in from Europe. Our people have to stay at home today and there is no relief and no work. The displaced persons are coming in. I have had complaints about that. They are taking the work that our people ordinarily would be exported to take. I know that is not a nice way to put it, but it is an actual fact. The freight rate increase further aggravates that situation so far as the maritimes are concerned.
I do not think the 21 per cent increase is the answer. I noticed in a press report that in the month of February alone the deficit on the Canadian National Railways amounted to $730,000. If that is true; if that is the monthly deficit on the Canadian National Railways the 21 per cent increase is not the answer. It will bring in only $70,000,000 a year on the basis of the present traffic. If the Canadian National Railways are accumulating a deficit of $730,000 monthly they will still be in the hole. The increase granted is not the answer. One needs to ask, is the railway inefficient? Is it obsolete? Surely, something is wrong with it and it needs to be overhauled. We cannot continue to pile on the backs of the consumers of this country a load of taxation in the form of an increased cost of living-and it is taxation, no matter how you look at it

for the maintenance of obsolete equipment. If there was an answer in this increase I would say, yes, perhaps it is all right; but there is no answer there. The institution is still uneconomic.
As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, the bonds that hold us together from coast to coast are these bands of steel. They are pretty shaky so far as the maritimes are concerned. I wonder whether the minister has ever taken a ride from Moncton to Sydney.

Take a ride down there some time, but take a belt and a life preserver with you, because you will need the belt when you go around the curves and you may need the life preserver on the strait of Canso. That is a pretty shaky stretch of road. I have never seen the service worse in the last thirty years than it has been in the last year or two. From Truro east, at least, it is terrible. The equipment is obsolete. They have no engines. I came up one night and the train was only five hours late. Why was she late? Well, she was late because she had to stop at Antigonish and leave the passengers on the train while she went away about fifteen miles looking for a car of salt.

My second question is, has the cabinet considered, or will it consider the appeal made by the seven provinces of Canada which are opposed to this increase that there be a stay of execution for thirty days to give each of these provinces an opportunity of appealing to the courts of the country against this proposed increase? I shall be obliged if the minister gives us that information.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to deal with the evidence as prepared and presented by the legal representatives of the various provinces, nor do I feel what I shall say will have any effect on the decision of the board of transport commissioners. However, since the west, through the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), has spoken on behalf of British Columbia, I thought I should add my voice from the east with regard to the reaction of the people of that section of the country.
Like other hon. members, I have just returned from my constituency. When this decision was made known I was in Halifax. I hope that the motion which was introduced today by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the remarks of the various hon. members, who have presented their views from various angles, will have some effect on the board of transport commissioners. If not, I hope and I believe that it will have some effect on the government in making them realize that this action is not one which is well received in other than the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
I think the point has been well taken by other hon. members that there was really no reason for Ontario and Quebec to present an argument against this increase. We all know that the industrial activity of our country is centred in these two provinces, and largely in Ontario. The same is true of our population. Quebec has a population of 3,331,882, while Ontario has a population of 3,787,655, or a total of 7,119,537 in these two provinces out of 11,500,000 people. The figures I have quoted are taken from the 1941 census. Very largely the same proportion exists today. Therefore I say I am not approaching this problem from the point of view of a legal argument, or as to whether the railways were justified in asking for an increase of 30 per cent.
As a businessman I recognize what has been said by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), that unless you have sufficient revenues you cannot operate successfully. That is recognized, but I do say that is a problem which the government must face if they are to carry out the very foundation of
Freight Rates

confederation. Using the same words that have already been used twice before, I believe that we should have something stronger than steel rails connecting east and west, and I agree with those who say that the whole economy of our nation is founded upon the individual economy of every province. You cannot have a prosperous central Canada, Ontario and Quebec, at the expense of other sections of the country. I do not say that in any unkind spirit with reference to the progressive and aggressive manner in which Ontario has gone about its industrial activities. I say it rather to point out that there are, in the extreme east and in the extreme west, disabilities that must be overcome.
I do not propose to deal with the political issue introduced by the hon. member for Waterloo South, nor shall I discuss the reply made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). All hon. members know my position with respect to free enterprise and competition. In this regard I differ from some hon. members, because I believe that competition will bring about greater efficiency and, in consequence of that increased efficiency, greater economy.
The Canadian National Railways are a publicly owned railway system and, because of the large returns secured in 1947, the people of the maritime provinces find it a little difficult to understand why this large increase was found necessary. A Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa on April 4 stated:
Canadian rails move largest peace freight.
Canadian railways last year carried the highest volume of freight ever moved in peacetime, the bureau of statistics reported. The railways moved 452,706,006 tons of goods in 1947. The total was exceeded only in two wartime years, 1943 and 1944, when 152,942,000 tons and 154,845,006 tons were transported. A gain of 14,000,060' tons was reported over 1946.
Then they refer to the freight which was carried. The largest increase was in grains, ores, petroleum, lumber, iron, steel, building materials, automobiles and newsprint. If you consider the freight carried you will find that the great proportion of it originates in central Canada. As regards automobiles, we are all aware, of course, of the large amount of freight which is carried by the railways from the automobile districts. Declines were shown in the movement of hay, straw, apples, cattle, sheep, wool, coal, coke and fresh fish, and these are products which come from the maritime provinces.
You will see why we in the maritimes are concerned about this increase. I do not propose to discuss the various royal commissions which have looked into the economy of the country, particularly as related to the mari-

times; but we do know that from time to time, without exception, before every royal commission that has investigated this subject the question of transportation from east to west has been a very live issue. Later on I shall read from one or two of the recommendations and findings, but it is generally accepted that there has been and is a disability, so far as transportation is concerned, from the point of view of the maritime provinces.
My approach to the consideration of this question is from the point of view of the promise that was made to us at the time of confederation. There is no question that we were given to understand, at the time of confederation in 1867, that we would have a line of communication whereby we would be able to trade with other parts of the country, and the reason advanced then was that it would improve the economic position of the east, and also promote settlement in the west. It did precisely that, so far as the west is concerned, because it resulted in carrying people to the west and to central Canada, and it was only natural that, with the large increase of population they had, they should gradually become an industrial centre.
With that background I feel justified in making this statement, and I do not as a rule use harsh terms. I say that there was a grave violation, if not of the terms of the confederation, at least of its spirit.

In the construction of trans-Canada railway lines east and west, I believe the fathers of confederation had that in mind. It was not merely a question of carrying passengers but the effect which the construction of railways would have on every part of the country. I think we should bear that in mind. I know that thought is a little bit new to the hon. member who asked the question, but it. is worthy of consideration. As he usually gives these matters study, I would suggest that he spend this evening and perhaps some time tomorrow in thinking it over. Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had already placed before lion, members my views with respect to the Increased freight rates announced by the board of transport commissioners. I had almost concluded my remarks, with the exception of summing up. It will be recalled that I had covered briefly the background of our transportation system from confederation in 1867 to today. I do not propose to go over that ground again, or to do more than briefly refer to one or two of the recommendations which may have been made. I had also given the reasons for the linking up of the provinces as outlined on more than one occasion by those who appeared and presented briefs before the various commissions which have been held to consider this question.
I had referred to royal commissions held from time to time which dealt with the disabilities of different sections of Canada and which had emphasized particularly those of Nova Scotia. I emphasized that not only should questions of revenues and expenditures be considered, but that trade and equality in all sections of the country-not in any . particular one alone-should be taken into .consideration.

speechtext:
I am pleased to know that; the hon. member has always been most kind when I have taken part in debates.
I referred to the fact that not only was settlement in the west promoted by the building of the railways, but that also activities in the east had been stimulated. Railway connections with the prairies gave a tremendous degree of assistance to the industrialization of Ontario and Quebec, and to the coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia as well as to lumbering in British Columbia. The railways in effect reduced the vast size of our country to one of reasonable proportions.
I had drawn attention to recommendations made in 1926 to the royal commission which dealt particularly with disabilities affecting Nova Scotia. May I quote briefly from the economic inquiry of 1934, which closes with this passage:
It -was partly for this reason that, in 1926, the royal commission on maritime claims was appointed. In its report the commission makes the following statement:
"We have come very definitely to the conclusion that the rate structure as it has been altered since 1912 has placed upon the trade and commerce of the maritime provinces (a) a burden which, as we have read the pronouncements and obligations undertaken at confederation, it was never intended it should bear; and (b) a burden which is, in effect, responsible in very considerable measure for depressing abnormally in the maritdmes today, business enterprise which had originated and developed before 1912- on the basis and faith of the rate structure as it then stood."
Thus we see that the claim of the maritime provinces, and in this instance more particularly that of Nova Scotia, was recognized. And it is because of that recognition we are fearful today of the effect this increased freight rate will have upon the economy of our section of the country.
Another brief prepared by the late Norman McL. Rogers and presented to the royal commission on the disabilities of Nova Scotia within the Canadian confederation stated as follows, in reference to the handicap under which the province of Nova Scotia was operating:
This handicap, arising in part from the interrelation of tariff policy and freight rates, appears to have been recognized by the royal commission on maritime claims in 1926, although the phraseology used by the commissioners would seem to suggest that it w-as recognized more particularly in relation to producers of the maritime provinces who wished to market their goods in central Canada. In section 2 of the report of the royal commission, the following references may be quoted as bearing upon this question:
"In addition, the ease which the maritime provinces have already submitted to the railway commission also raises the question of handicaps

Freight Rales
arising from the geographical position of their natural products and their distance, generally, from the central markets."
I have every reason to believe that the reference to "central markets" is a reference to the markets of Ontario and Quebec, to which I referred on more than one occasion this afternoon. Then, to continue with the quotation:
"We are far from suggesting that there should be interference on the part of the railway commission with the business judgment of the railway companies, or that there should be any confusion between trade development that can reasonably be expected from the railway rate structure, and trade development that must be a matter for public or government responsibility quite apart from rate structure."
I pause there to repeat to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the two words "government responsibility" as they appear in this report.
I felt I was justified in bringing this matter before the government today in the hope that not only would it consider the revenues and expenditures of the railway systems as placed before the board of transport commissioners at board hearings, but rather that it would deal with the matter from the point of view of the effect it would have upon all sections of Canada, and particularly, of course, upon Nova Scotia and Halifax, which I have the honour to represent.
In closing, may I place greater emphasis upon what I said this afternoon. Our transportation system is the means of linking the economic activities, developments and progress of our country. It must not be considered from the point of view of revenues and expenditures only; but matters of trade, and the effect which certain procedures may have on our trade expansion in every section of Canada, and not only the central section, must be considered.
I made reference this afternoon to the effect the change in rate is having on the extreme western section of our country, and in this I have supported the thought expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I say again that the same effect is being felt in the maritimes. Apart from the financial and legal aspects of the case as presented by seven out of the nine provinces, I submit that the spirit in which we entered confederation should ever be kept before us if we are to have a united, contented and satisfied nation.
I opened my remarks this afternoon by saying that I did not know what effect any remarks of mine would have in delaying the bringing into effect of the increases on April 8, but I felt that at least I was doing my duty
in placing the views which I held, and which I believed were held not alone in my native province of Nova Scotia tut from the information given me by hon. members from other provinces, throughout the whole eastern maritimes. I ask the Minister of Transport and, through him, the government to give serious thought to the suggestions I offered this afternoon with a view to either holding up this increase or formulating some plan to offset the ill effects which I believe will be felt in the extreme sections of our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a subject which is important to all Canada and particularly important to the maritime provinces. I arrived back from Nova Scotia only an hour before the house convened this afternoon. I did not know this subject was coming up and I did not have an opportunity to make any preparation. However, I feel that I should express my views. I am particularly pleased to be associated with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) speaking after each other and joining forces in giving the viewpoint of our part of Canada.
I do not think this important matter should be discussed under these conditions. We should have had some notice. As far as I am concerned, I have not had an opportunity to get a copy of the finding of the board of transport commissioners. I think every hon. member is entitled to have had a printed copy so that he can examine it and not have to rely upon casual references in the press. Before we were called upon to discuss this matter we should have had a pronouncement of policy by the government. The minister may say what he likes but the government cannot divorce themselves from responsibility in the subject we are now discussing, as the board of transport commissioners is appointed by and responsible to them.
Freight Rates

There is a second point in connection with the short view which I would emphasize, and it is this. As far as the prairie provinces are concerned, this 21 per cent increase is a direct charge on the farmers of the prairies at a time when they are hampered in their attempts to offset and to meet it by being under a series of prohibitions and controls which make the levy most onerous at the present time. I do not care whether you call these controls agreements or export embargoes, or what the device is by which you limit the amount the producer can get for that which he has to sell, or when his markets are restricted in which he is able to sell that which he produces. That, by whatever name you call it, is in effect a control. Therefore, if it should be that this cause is finally lost; if the protests of the seven provinces are not to be heeded and there is to be this added burden, this aggravation of what some of us in the western part of Canada are coming to regard as a second-class citizenship; if that is to be the case, then I urge, with all the earnestness I can command, that this increase be not imposed until such time as those in western agriculture are freely able to sell those things which they produce for what they can get for them in whatever markets they may seek.
There is a long view. I said at the beginning that in my view a clear case was made out against the need of relieving the financial situation of the railroads by the imposition of higher freight rates now. I do not suppose there is in the business world anywhere today anything quite so haphazard, unscientific and un-understandable as are the current schedules of freight rates. I have had the experience in committees of this house of having highly placed officers of the railways admit that freight tariffs have simply grown like Topsy and that they are complicated, unscientific and unwieldy.
I venture to say that there are not more than half a dozen lawyers in the Dominion of Canada who are qualified to interpret with authority the rate structure of either railroad. I doubt very much whether there are half a dozen. I have some knowledge of the business world, and people in our part of the country who are in business are frequent and, continuous users of freight transportation. Any firm that is doing business to any considerable extent and is shipping is simply crazy if it does not retain, as in fact it does retain at substantial salaries, men whose job it is to keep in touch with the freight rate structures and to find out how they can do business and what it will cost them to do business. There are classifications and cross-classifications. I have looked at them. The last volume I saw was a thick one, the
fMr. Mutch.]
so-called revised edition by one railroad. No one person on earth knew what was in it. The railroads themselves maintain, at every major shipping point in this country, men whose job it is to pass on these rates and classifications. All credit to the railways for that. The instructions which these men have are that they shall see to it that the shipper gets the best deal under the freight rates which are available to him and to make helpful suggestions. Because of the fact that they are as complicated as they are, that is the situation.
I have not dealt for the moment with the regional discriminations, with the horse-trading and the dealing which has taken place over the years with respect to local areas. Rates are purchased by concessions made at the time but which it seems we are to continue to pay forever. I think what we would be better advised to do is to suspend the operation of these increases until such a time as we have something more nearly approaching a free economy in western Canada for our farmers and importers generally; and the government, through its own agencies or through the board of transport commissioners, could begin now, at this late date, to see what is equitable in the matter of freight rates in this country. If we do not do so, what will happen?
Someone has spoken today about the steel rails that bind the country together. Someone else said that there is a much more important element than steel rails that holds us together. Railways made possible our first communications, and the presumption was that because we have been able to travel up and down on the railways, we now all love each other and have a common bond in our citizenship. Actually the type of thing which has been going on since the early development of the west, the discrimination against our areas by the railways -even by the railway which is the creature, the servant and the property of the people themselves-as a result of the rulings of the board, has done very little to consolidate the people of Canada. The railways have done more in the opposite direction by this type of discrimination, this type of charging all that the traffic will bear, where you can get it; not because the people are easy-going, have more money than those elsewhere, are stupid or anything like that, but because of dire necessity, because they must have certain things and because there is no other way of getting them: and for that which you must have, you pay what you must pay in order to get it. This has been the situation.
We know perfectly well where the burden of the 21 per cent increase in freight rates will fall. It will fall not on those who are best able to pay it but on those who are least able.

Freight Rates
My complaint is not that once more we of the west and indeed those in the maritimes- we of the seven provinces, shall I say, who have expressed a willingness to get together and to make some contribution to the building up of nationhood and the consolidation of good feeling in this country-are to be left without those benefits which we desire because two of the stronger provinces refuse to co-operate. That is understandable on the basis perhaps of thoughtful though misguided selfishness. However, I am a little bit at a loss to understand why in a situation like this, these same two provinces have adopted in this matter the role of the Levite. Not being themselves affected, they have passed by on the other side instead of taking advantage of the opportunity to help the weaker provinces to win some consideration for themselves.
I have a shrewd suspicion, Mr. Speaker, that for the moment, in appealing to these provinces, I am pleading a lost cause. Sir, I would not want to go back to my home city, to my home province or to western Canada generally, and have it said of me that I had been unable or unwilling to rise in my place in this house and give voice to the resentment which I feel with regard to the timing, the method and the result of the investigation generally. I think it is tremendously important, even though we lose out, that as an evidence of good faith the government should exercise that authority which it undoubtedly has to delay the implementing of these new rates until the least of the provinces shall have had a full opportunity to present the views of their people in the one place where they can go in these matters, namely to the federal government. If necessary', and if they desire it, failing satisfaction there, there should be delay until they have had an opportunity of seeking satisfaction in the courts themselves. I think this delay, in all fairness and in all justice, should be made.
I come back once again to that other thought to which I gave voice.
Failing successful appeal, if it is decided that this impost must go on, then so far as this government is concerned, I urge that they meet the situation which they cannot escape seeing, by freeing western agriculture from the shackles which are on it and give the west every opportunity to pay the extra tariff imposed upon them.

speechtext:
Yes, and from
Alberta; and well made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka). The minister now has representations from all the provinces affected by this discriminatory rate structure. And, after all, I should have thought that by this time the minister would have removed the veil and allowed us in the House of Commons to have some idea as to what the government's stand in this matter is. The responsibility is not that of the board of transport commissioners. That responsibility rests on the government, and on no other. I am going to refer to the act, for no amount of casuistry can get away from this fact, that the government must assume the responsibility. If it had appointed a committee of parliament, it might wait until the committee reported before doing anything. If it had appointed a royal commission it could have said, "After all, this is merely a recommendation." But it appointed the board of transport commissioners, under law, and the matter was submitted to that board.
I shall now refer to the relative sections. First, the board is composed of six members, holding office during good behaviour for the period of ten years from the date of appointment, but may be removed at any time by the governor in council upon address of the Senate and the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Is what they have done "good behaviour"?

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Then we come on to decisions of the board, where it is stated that decisions of the board are final, unless they are reviewed, rescinded, altered or varied by the board itself, which may rehear any
f Mr. Diefenbaker.]
application before coming to a final decision. However, where there is no rehearing, we find that section 52 of the Railway Act states:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order which the governor in council may make with respect thereto shall be binding upon, the board and upon all parties.
Not only have there been representations made by various provinces, but I understand that representations have been made by various parties affected. So that the responsibility rests-and I repeat this-upon the governor in council or, in other words, upon the cabinet.
There is provision for appeal; but the facts in this case, if I understand them correctly, permit of no appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The act states:
An appeal shall lie from the board to the Supreme Court of Canada upon a question of jurisdiction, upon leave therefor being obtained from a judge of the said court-
And again:
An appeal shall also lie from the board to such court upon any question which in the opinion of the board is a question of law, or a question of jurisdiction, or both . . .
There is no question here either of law or of jurisdiction. My recollection is-and I speak subject to correction by the minister-that the question of jurisdiction was raised at one time during the proceedings before the board, and that an application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada on the ground of jurisdiction was in fact dismissed.
So that however much the minister may endeavour to evade responsibility, the responsibility for what will take place under this recommendation, or advisory recommendation if you will, will rest upon the government which, alone, will be responsible for permitting this recommendation to be carried into effect.
The baby is on the government's doorstep. It cannot in any way divest itself of its responsibility. Surely by this time, after the arguments advanced here today, the minister is or should be in a position to let the house and the country know the course the government intends to follow.
I am not going to enter into any argument as to the advantage of private enterprise over socialism, although that was brought into debate today. One of these times it will have to be answered. I want to get down to the

Freight Rates
meat of this situation, as I see it. Members from the maritimes-at least those who are interested-have set forth their view that there is diserimination. By reason of the mountain differential there is discrimination in British Columbia. There is discrimination on the prairies where the effective rates in the three prairie provinces are above the average level of Ontario and Quebec to the extent of some 14 per cent. That discrimination, under the 21 per cent across-the-board increase in freight rates will be increased until it will amount, over all, to 16-94 per cent. In other words, by this over-all increase the prairie provinces are being penalized by an additional 2-94 per cent over what they are paying today.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), who has just arrived this evening, has certain representations to make with respect to British Columbia. However, by reason of the fact that the list of speakers is complete, he finds himself unable to make those representations on this occasion and has authorized me to place some facts before the house on his behalf. I do so, accepting these representations as being proper in every respect and as being the representations he would have made respecting the situation in British Columbia.
The Vancouver Daily Province of April 1 points out that, according to an estimate made by A. K. Lloyd, president and general manager of B.C. Tree Fruits Limited, the 21 per cent rail freight boost may cost British Columbia's fruit industry $1,000,000 a year. By this 21 per cent increase across the board the mountain differential is made even worse than it is today. The situation today is that one and a quarter miles in the mountains equals one mile elsewhere, and a 21 per cent increase on the one-quarter mile will mean an increase in the discrimination against British Columbia, a discrimination that will affect practically all the products produced in that province. The hon. member also handed me, and I now place it before the house, a telegram which he received from the Okanagan and main line associated boards of trade. The telegram is dated April 3 from Enderby, B.C., and reads:
General Pearkes, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Strongly urge dominion government notify board transport commissioners that any attempt to increase rates on British Columbia traffic before existing discriminatory mountain differential removed will be appealed to highest authority.
I point out again that the only authority to whom an appeal can be made is to the governor in council the government of Canada. There is no appeal to the supreme
court or any other judicial body except on a question of law or on a question of jurisdiction, and the latter matter has already been determined.
I now return to the prairie provinces and their views. We in the prairie provinces, without regard to party considerations, view any increase across the board as an intensification of the freight rates discrimination that has existed over the years and against which successive governments in the various provinces have objected. I feel that the effect of the board's decision will be to perpetuate the blight of discrimination against the prairies, against British Columbia and against the maritimes.
We in the prairie provinces and those who live in the maritime provinces have much in common in this regard. Discriminatory freight rates have had the result of relegating some provinces to the position of second-class provinces in the economic set-up of this dominion. Discriminatory freight rates have devitalized the potentialities of industrial expansion in (he prairie provinces and in the maritimes.
During the war we on the prairies were penalized. During that period we were denied any real participation in the billions of dollars that were advanced by the government for the development of war industries, not because of a lack of natural resources but because of the discriminatory nature of our freight rates and because we could not interest the government in decentralizing industry. This is a matter of great moment at this time when we find ourselves in the midst of world turmoil.
I believe the time has come, not to have an across-the-board increase in freight rates which will merely continue if not perpetuate-the unfairness under which these various provinces suffer today, but to have a scientific revamping of the freight rate structure. Instead of doing that, the board has recommended the easy way, it has simply added all annex to an already dilapidated structure. During the course of his remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg South pointed out that he did not think there were more than six men in the dominion who understood the structure of freight rate differentials.

speechtext:
He said six lawyers; after all, he was taking the best men in Canada when he referred to the legal profession. That is true. We have a board of transport commissioners, and I suggest to the minister that, having regard to what this
Freight Rates

increase in freight rates will do at this time to interfere with the economy of the country, he should apply the veto on the part of this government to the immediate operation of these recommendations and place the board of transport commissioners in a position where, with the necessary scientific ability they have available, they can revamp our freight rates structure, to the end that one of the most serious disadvantages under which some of the provinces in confederation are operating will be removed once and for all.
When the discrimination is removed there can be no objections to such increases as are necessary to assure a fair and proper return to the railroad companies. No one wants a condition of affairs where deficits will continue. Having regard to the situation in which our country is today, I am sure that no one desires to see continued this discrimination which has done more to put east against the west and to separate our country than any other single thing.
I suggest to the minister that the responsibility rests with him. He will never have a united federation; he will never build the type of Canada that we want to see -built, where every part of the country is developed according to the resources it possesses, until this unfairness is removed. He will never build the kind of Canada that will assure the destiny that Canada should achieve by having some of the provinces placed in the position where, through the years, they will continue to be "have not" provinces industrially. The minister has the opportunity to do that which over the years many successive ministers of railways have realized should be done but have never had an opportunity of doing or have never had the vision to do. They never had the opportunity to do what the hon. gentleman who now holds the portfolio can do for Canada as a whole.
This is not a party matter. If this matter were allowed to come to a vote removed from all the trammels of party consideration; if each and every member voted not on the basis of voting non-confidence in the government but on the basis of the views he held, you would be surprised, Mr. Speaker, by the result. This afternoon when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke a most unusual thing occurred; there was applause from the government side of the house for many of the arguments which he advanced. That applause, could not have been missed by the Minister of Transport. That applause represented an expression of the inward ideas of hon. members across this dominion who, without regard to any consideration, unselfishly

want to see Canada developed as a unit rather than to be Balkanized industrially by reason of a differential that denies equality as between British Columbia and Ontario, that denies equality as between Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec, that denies equality as between the maritimes and central Canada. Those inequalities are inequities and those inequities are doing more to separate this country and, in the event of war, to make it defenceless by reason of the centralization of industry in central Canada. These inequalities and inequities would be removed if the minister would either place the matter in the hands of the transport commissioners, with all the thousands and thousands of pages of evidence that they have before them and knowing the facts as they do, or set up a commission to take additional evidence with a view to removing this discrimination, for, as long as it continues, this country can never hope to achieve that development she should have, having regard to the resources she possesses.

Every farmer in my riding is being penalized by this increased freight rate. Every poultryman is being penalized two cents a dozen on eggs. The. berry growers are penalized on some 15,000,000 pounds of fruit which they will ship this year. The. previous speaker mentioned wires that he had received. We believe that we are going to change, the policy. I have always been a sort of modest member who has refrained from saying what he. thinks, but I can assure the government that if some of my legal friends, the hon. member for Lake Centre or some other member of his profession can show me how a motion can be
introduced that will present this issue straight to the house, at least three British Columbia members will, vote in favour of the motion, even if it should be a want of confidence motion, because we believe that the very future of our province is at stake in this matter. We believe, not in appeals such as the hon. member for Lake Centre suggested, but that parliament should be supreme in this matter. I do not know much about the. rules. I never break them myself; I know that my hon. friend the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maelnnis) is an expert on the rules and that he sometimes calls me to order, but I believe that on this question we are in agreement. I want to impress on the government, and it will continue to be impressed on the government by the private members from British Columbia both in public and in private, that no longer are we going to stand to be. sacrificed for the benefit of Ontario and Quebec, nor do I believe that the people in the maritimes will continue to. be sacrificed in this way. I want to impress on the minister, who I believe is both capable and fair-minded, the necessity of a change of apparent government policy on this question, for without a change you cannot maintain unity within Canada or deal out justice to all parts of this country. I am for once disappointed that we have not heard on this question from the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who usually speaks every three minutes on every third question, but I notice a great silence today from Ontario and Quebec on this subject. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel somewhat diffident in following the able speech of the modest member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), with most though not all of whose remarks I agree. He stated, however, that the British Columbia members have not received much support from the maritime provinces.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I said on this side of the house.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I beg the hon. member's pardon, because I was going to point out that the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) and my seatmate the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) have already spoken
Freight Rates

in support of his stand. They presented very strong arguments, indeed most of the arguments which I was going to use myself. But as no one from New Brunswick has spoken I should like to indicate to the house that in my province we feel keenly about this freight rate increase. One has only to read the newspapers of the last week or to talk with men from different parts of the province to realize how strong the feeling is.
Freight rates have always been an acute problem in the maritime provinces. It has been said in fact that the freight rate means life or death to maritime industry. This has been so in the past and we feel that it applies also to the future. Over a long period of years we have lost industries in the maritimes because of high freight rates, and as the hon. member for Cumberland pointed out this evening, we have also lost many thousands of our people. Our people have to go where they can find work, where there is industry, and if industry leaves any part of the country the people have to leave too. That has been the result in our province ever since confederation.
It is not necessary for me to go into the history of freight rates in the maritime provinces because they were dealt with this afternoon. Our people have always been conscious of our difficulties before and ever since we joined confederation. One of the reasons our province came into confederation was the promise that freight rates would be one of the main considerations. We were not in confederation very long until we began to realize that the freight rate structure of this country was against these little provinces down by the sea, and we began at once to lose our industry and also our people to the central parts of Canada.
In 1925 there was formed in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island what was known as the maritime transportation commission. This commission received the support of the governments of the three maritime provinces. It also received the support of all the businessmen in the three provinces. The idea of this maritime transportation commission, was, among other things, to keep careful watch on the freight rate situation in these provinces. Out of the idea of this maritime transportation commission eventually developed the Duncan commission which made certain recommendations for our provinces with relation to freight rates, which recommendations were not carried out to their full extent, with the result that we continued to lose industry and our people, even though under the Maritime

Freight Rates Act we had a 20 per cent benefit over the other parts of Canada with the exception of the west.
What does this increase of 21 per cent mean now? Mr. Rand Matheson, who was the manager of the maritime transportation commission, has estimated that it will mean between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 to the people of these three provinces; that is, that it will cost our fishermen, our farmers, our people in industry and our lumbermen an extra amount of between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000. It will cost the whole of Canada something like $70,000,000. We have not one-tenth of the population in the maritime provinces. It is estimated that there are about thirteen million people in Canada today. In the maritime provinces we have less than one million people, and if we were to pay on the basis of our population we would contribute only one-thirteenth of this amount of $70,000,000; but, according to the estimate of Mr. Matheson, and he is a keen authority on railway matters, we are contributing one-seventh of the amount, which, in itself, is inequitable. This will increase the cost to the farmers. Someone pointed out this afternoon that it will mean a great increase in the cost of the machinery we have to buy from central Canada. It will mean an increase in the cost of the fertilizer which the farmer uses. In New Brunswick we use something like 60,000 tons of fertilizer a year. It will mean an increase in the cost of practically everything that goes into the farming industry. It will mean an increase in the cost of feed grains which we have to use in our dairy and hog industry.
Take an industry like the Atlantic Sugar Refinery in the city of Saint John. A few days ago the senior hon. member for Halifax was bewailing the fact, and rightly so, that during the last few years the sugar refinery in the city of Halifax had moved to the city of Montreal. What will happen to an industry like the Atlantic Sugar Refinery in Saint John with these increased freight rates? We know what has happened in the past. It will mean only a few years until this industry is closed up and moves to some other part of Canada. That is what we in New Brunswick and in the maritime provinces generally have had to put up with for years, and it seems to be the logical result of the increase in freight rates.
I could go on and mention other industries. The hon. member for Cumberland mentioned the stove and furnace industry, which is in my own province in the town of Sackville. It employs quite a number of people. These

Freight Rates
people have to bring a lot of their products for the manufacture of their stoves from central Canada. This cannot go on forever. If the freight rates are to be increased they will have to move nearer to the great centres of population in this dominion. And so it goes on, first one industry and then another. The main reason why we lose these industries in our province is the freight rates.
I read an article the other day in which the Premier of Prince Edward Island said that the potato industry in Prince Edward Island would be very hard hit. As a matter of fact, I think it was the deputy minister of agriculture of Prince Edward Island who made this statement:
The "very existence" of Prince Edward Island farmers was threatened by the 21 per cent increase in freight rates granted the railways by the board of transport commissioners' ruling this week, a resolution adopted at the annual meeting of the P.E.I. Potato' Growers' Association declared. The resolution urged that the case for the maritimes be reviewed.
What is true of Prince Edward1 Island; with reference to potatoes would be also true in the province of Nova Scotia with reference to apples, I believe, and in the province' of New Brunswick as well. Under the British empire trade agreements, Nova Scotia sold its apples to England1. That province had a splendid market there. That market is being lost to the apple growers of Nova Scotia, with the result that they will have to seek a market in central Canada and in other parts of Canada, and this increase in freight rates will be a severe blow to the apple growers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
I could go on and quote case after case, but I do not think it is necessary because of what has been said1 this afternoon and evening. I would point out that if all sections of Canada were equally prosperous, if we were as prosperous in the maritimes as are the people in Ontario and Quebec, we would have no objection to bearing our share of this freight rate increase, and there would be no argument against it. We in the maritime provinces have not been as prosperous as the people in other parts of Canada; we have not been as prosperous for the very reasons that I have been pointing out, and one of the main ones has been the increase in freight rates. For instance, our farmers in the maritime provinces and in New Brunswick particularly received an average salary last year of about $800. The average salary for the whole of Canada was about $1,700. Thus our people received one-half of what the farmers throughout Canada received. The same thing applies to other industries as well. That is the point
I am trying to make. If our people were as prosperous as are the people in parts of central Canada, then we would have no objection to bearing our just portion of the burden.
I think it was very well put this afternoon that this is not a matter for a commission to decide. This is a very broad question. It is a question which affects the very life of this dominion of ours; it affects the unity of our people, and it is something which the government of this country must decide. The decision must not be left with any commission,
I should like to call attention to what the Premier of New Brunswick said in this connection a short time ago. It is as follows:
McNair urges joint action
Suggests Ottawa delay operation of freight boost.
In the course of his remarks he had this to say:
It was clearly intended under the Maritime Freight Rates Act that the maritime provinces should be placed in a position to do business with the other provinces of Canada. Any movement or action which has the effect of disrupting this position is most disturbing.
Then further:
I am strongly of the opinion that the federal government should intervene to ensure that at least thirty days' notice be given by the railways before putting into effect the rates permitted under the recent decision.
He thinks there should not be any hurry in this matter but that there should be time for careful consideration. The Premier of Nova Scotia, the Hon. Angus Macdonald, said:
The new rates recommended by the board run contrary to the spirit of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and, in my judgment, the board has failed to deal adequately with the arguments made by maritime counsel on this point.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the government that these men whom I have quoted this evening, the Premier of New Brunswick, the Premier of Nova Scotia and the Premier of Prince Edward Island, are all very strong supporters of the present administration at Ottawa. If it were some years ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, "Not a five cent piece to a Tory province", we might understand the attitude the government has taken. But here we have three premiers who are very strong supporters of this present administration, and each of them has stated definitely that this is a problem which the federal government should solve and which, in justice to the people of their provinces, must receive immediate attention.
