subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a difficult debate in which to take part, largely because all the debating is on one side. Although I presume there is a different point of view on the question, there appears to be no one to give expression to that point of view. I merely rise-and it is almost inevitable at this stage of the debate-[DOT] to emphasize some of the points that have already been made. It is difficult at this stage to make any new points. Before I go on with what I have to say, I wish to refer to a point raised by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) and also by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black); that is, that it is too bad that the debate came up in the way it did, namely, on a motion to adjourn the house on a matter of urgent public importance.
I too regret that the debate had to come up in that way. Unfortunately in this house we have not reached the stage where a member can rise in his place and ask the government to set aside a certain time for debating an important question. That is the procedure at Westminster. There they have a standing order similar to our standing order 31; but as regards any question of importance arising, the leader of the opposition or a private member, either on the government side or on the opposition side of the house, can rise and ask that a day be set aside for discussing the question, and invariably that is done.
The leader of this party could not in the natural order of things have given more notice than he did. As a matter of fact we did a very unusual thing. We not only notified the Speaker, which we are not obliged to do under the rule, but we notified the government's chief whip and the leaders of the other parties as well, because we appreciated that this was a matter of which they should have some notice and that it was not in any sense a political matter. That is the reason the question has come up in this way.
As I understand the freight rates question as it affects British Columbia, it is a matter of the fairness of the rates; and may I say by the way that in this matter I can speak both as a maritimer and as a member from British Columbia. Like so many others, I had to leave the maritimes in order to make my livelihood somewhere else, and I therefore know their difficulties there. As I understand the question in British Columbia, it is not that we are opposed to an increase in freight rates if that increase is necessary, but we object to the fact that the decision made at this time perpetuates freight rates which we have considered for years to be inequitable. That is the point.

I have lived for forty years in British Columbia; in every year during that time that province has been fighting at Ottawa for a better break in the matter of freight rates and wTe have not got it yet. Not only that; but this order, if it stands as it is now, will make the situation worse than it was before. Not that the present discrimination will be increased by 21 per cent, but it will be more than it was before. That is the position as we see it in British Columbia.
It has been mentioned that the railways were represented b}'. I was going to say some of the best lawyers in Canada, but I will say some of the cleverest lawyers. One of them made the statement in argument that the inquiry into freight rates was concerned with revenue for the railways. He said that the board of transport commissioners was limited to the fixing of just and reasonable rates, and he said further that:
. . . just and reasonable rates referred to in the statute are rates that must be just and reasonable to the railways to whom they are to be paid, and that unremunerative rates are unjust and unreasonable.
I maintain there is more involved here than simply revenue for the railways. That, of course, is important because, without the necessary revenue, they cannot carry on and serve the country, but there is more than that involved. The railways in Canada were built in order to develop the various parts of this far-flung country and to knit the provinces together and that is where in my opinion the government comes in. Even if the board of transport commissioners is restricted to dealing solely with the question of revenue for the railways, without regard to whether the collection of that revenue is equitable or not, the government is bound to take notice of that, and that is what I suggest to the minister and to the government that they must do.
Let me say again that, as I understand the position of the people of British Columbia, they are not opposed to an increase in freight rates as such. They are opposed to the maintenance of an inequitable freight structure. I have in my hand, and I was going to read it to the house, a copy of the wire that was read by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he spoke on behalf of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). That wire makes it quite clear that until the discriminatory mountain differential is removed, British Columbia will not be satisfied. We believe that since freight rates in our province are much higher than average, we should not be asked to pay higher rates until the rates have been increased in those areas which have for many years enjoyed the

Freight Rates
relatively lower rates. I submit that is not an unreasonable position to take. I imagine it is pretty much the position that the people of the nmritimes take as well. But if we continue the present discrimination, we are helping to create an imbalance in the economy of Canada, and we are certainly not helping to create that unity which must exist in this country if we are to be prosperous, happy and free. I was indeed glad to hear so many of those who spoke in this debate refer to the fact that in order to have unity we must have equality. We cannot have unity when certain sections of the country feel they are being discriminated against for the benefit of other sections. That being the case, if we want unity let us see to it that all sections of this country have the same consideration and the same opportunities.
I am glad tonight to be able to associate myself with those other members from British Columbia who have opposed the decision made by the board of transport commissioners.
I hope the government will not allow the decision to go into effect without having an opportunity for a review.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Having listened in this debate, Mr. Speaker, to all those who have spoken, representing most of the provinces of Canada, I thought, since I was the only Tory member from Prince Edward Island, I might be allowed an opportunity of saying a few words.
This question of transportation is one in which I have always been interested from the point of view of our own province. I have endeavoured to show the discrimination with reference to freight rates by all governments against our province as a province. But that is not quite the question with which we are dealing tonight.
To begin with, I might say that I did not approve the manner in which this debate was introduced into the house, but I approved the manner suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch). However, that is past and the last speaker has given the reason why the debate was so introduced. It does not give the members of this house the fullest opportunity to discuss the greatest question that has arisen in parliament for many years, namely, the freight rate increase which was announced a short time ago.
When this freight rate increase of 21 per cent was announced, with other entanglements, it rocked the maritime provinces and nearly shook them clear of the Dominion of Canada. It also rocked the western provinces to the same extent. The central provinces, owing to their great wealth and their centralization of great factories, have nothing much to say
with regard to it, because both the maritimes and the western provinces are paying the shot and the central provinces are enjoying the benefits.
There is one thing I want to mention-and it may not be quite in order-along the lines of what has been said by those who have spoken, and it is this. The board of transport commissioners had no authority that I can see, although I am not a lawyer, to make this increase without due consideration having been given and information having been received in this way. I believe this matter should have been discussed on the floor of the house before it ever went to the board of transport commissioners. They are not all-powerful. For instance, over a year ago I took objection to the board of transport commissioners and protested their going into our province and setting freight rates over which they have no jurisdiction whatever. I am glad to say that, after they went there, they themselves found out that they did not have the jurisdiction to submit to us freight rates that we should have to pay. I feel assured that the government should not have given this board of transport commissioners the authority to go over this country and set freight rates; I feel they are not getting the true picture of what we should have with reference to freight rates.
Of course there are two sides to this question. Two great railways are connected with it; in fact, two of the greatest railway systems in the world, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. However, these two companies are somewhat different. One is practically a government-owned railway and the other one is what we might call a private enterprise. Notwithstanding that, we have these two companies now to share and share alike in the decision of the board of transport commissioners; that is, each of them is entitled to put on this new rate for its own benefit. The Canadian National is a railway that Canadians are proud of. It was built, like the Canadian Pacific, for one purpose, namely, the development of Canada. The Canadian National is giving us excellent service, generally speaking, across Canada. If we are demanding still greater service from this railway, and also service in other directions throughout the country, if it cannot make revenue and operating expenses balance, there is only one solution. If we demand that the railway maintain the service at the highest possible level without the raising of rates, then the government must pay the deficit.
However, in the matter of freight rates, as in ordinary passenger transportation, there i3 the matter of differences of equipment. I was
Freight Rates

about to say with regard to the maritime provinces-and I would speak particularly about Prince Edward Island-that we lack the transportation system enjoyed by the other provinces. However we are gaining somewhat, and had hoped we would be linked up with the rest of Canada, and have de luxe trains such as have been provided by the Canadian National across the country.
How does the increase in freight rates affect Prince Edward Island? As an agricultural province, it will cast a heavier burden on Prince Edward Island than on any province. Freight rates will be increased on our exports as well as on our imports. We are exporters and importers. We have no great factories or industries. Our people must live by the soil and the fisheries. We have only two industries of any great importance. As some hon. members have said tonight, it can be well imagined that an increase in freight rates on our exports will almost cripple the farmers of Prince Edward Island.
Someone has placed on record figures showing estimates concerning these increases. Estimates have been made as to what it will cost Prince Edward Island farmers and fishermen-particularly the farmers-in the export of their goods. The amount has been set down at $1,500,000 to $2,000,000 as the amount the new increase will cost, if it goes into effect. However, while we are all talking against the increase in freight rates, and endeavouring to persuade the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)1 and the government that the increases ought not to be put into effect, I am positive that neither the minister nor the government would dare to put them into effect at the present time. They must be given consideration. From one end of Canada to the other, with the possible exception of the central provinces, a cry has been raised against them.
In face of that, and in face of the arguments submitted from time to time not only in the house, but when the investigation was taking place before the commission at different points across Canada, I feel that these increases will not be put into effect. All these things must have a bearing on the action the government will take. I certainly hope I am right when I say that it will not dare to impose these increases on the maritimes and the western provinces.
A few days ago I mentioned discriminations against those situated in geographically extreme locations. I mentioned, for instance, the freight rates we in the maritimes and those in the west have to pay on automobiles, trucks and farm machinery, none of which are manufactured in

the maritime provinces. If this increase were added, for an ordinary car brought from Oshawa, instead of paying $86 we would have to pay at least $100, and up as high as $165 to bring to Prince Edward Island a car that a farmer may wish to buy. I endeavoured the other day to show the discrimination in this instance; and the same could be said about all farm implements. The situation is that a farmer living near Oshawa will receive support from that factory, when he produces food for the men employed there, and their families. When that farmer buys a car he pays the factory price. We in Prince Edward Island also support the factories, but we get no direct results from the sale of produce, because those commodities are supplied by the local farmers. Yet, when we attempt to support that factory by buying an automobile or a truck we are discriminated against and penalized to the extent of from $100 to $165. This should be placed on the stamp rate, and there should be some equalization whereby a man living next door to a factory would not be in a position to buy his car one nickel cheaper than a man living in Prince Edward Island or in the west.
Some of the largest merchants have taken up this matter, and have equalized freight rates throughout Canada on the articles they manufacture. The matter of freight rates brings us to many other matters which, in the interests of our own provinces, we could discuss. I know, however, that the hour is late and that before the Minister of Transport speaks there are other hon. members who wish to make their contribution to the debate. I trust the minister will give the matter such consideration that those of us in the east will not have our hopes so terribly blasted, as they were when the 21 per cent increase was announced.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) referred to Prince Edward Island's voicing its opinion against these increases. It is not necessary for me to repeat what has been said by representatives from other provinces. The resolution passed by Prince Edward Island is already in the hands of the minister, and it is not necessary for me to repeat it at this time.
Let me say I am sure the government will give this matter its honest consideration, because it is entirely in the government's hands. We should not have to be ruled by the board; the government must take the responsibility for this increase in freight rates.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few things I should like to say at this time. I believe it was fortunate that I happened to be in Alberta, in my own constituency, at the time the freight rate increase was announced. Thus I was able to secure a

Freight Rates
-clear and concise picture of the reaction of many people in that part of Canada.
It will be noted, if one examines the press releases of March 30, that the board of transport commissioners authorized the railway companies to make a general advance in freight rates to the extent of 21 per cent, with certain exceptions. Those exceptions relate to grain and flour. Then we read that there was to be a flat increase of twenty-five cents a ton on coal and coke. We also find reference made to minimum charges for certain less than carload shipments between any two stations. We find further reference to recognized differentials by way of rail, water and so forth and the indication that those differentials are to be preserved.
While I do not desire to tie my remarks specifically to Alberta, I feel I am justified in taking that province as a typical example, possibly the most outstanding example of the discrimination which exists under the prevailing freight rate structure. As anyone who examines the facts will realize, Alberta suffers the highest freight rate charges on goods exported from that province and pays the highest rates -on goods coming in from any other part of Canada. Alberta stands at the apex of the freight rate structure, and I sometimes think that from that lofty position we are able, not only to have a better appreciation of our problem but to look down and note the problems confronting the maritime provinces, the other prairie provinces and British Columbia.
I think it is well to bear in mind that the prevailing freight rate structure in Canada, particularly in western Canada, was designed at a time when traffic was considerably less than it is at the present time and when the population of the west was quite sparse. I had always believed that freight rates or freight costs depended, at least in part, upon the volume of business available. However, we discover in western Canada that as the volume of business increased, as it multiplied many times over, there was no freight rate reduction commensurate with the greatly increased volume of business.
One could briefly list the disadvantages suffered by my own province under four or five different heads. We know that in Alberta as between two points, let us say 100 miles apart, we pay a much higher rate than is paid between two points in Ontario an equal number of miles apart. This afternoon the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) seemed to take exception to the suggestion that the provinces in central Canada must, in some measure at least, bear the responsibility for this situation. I should like to say to the hon. member that feeling definitely exists in
western Canada. I am saying that when one examines all the evidence he cannot avoid being convinced that the condition is approved by the provinces of central Canada.
I realize that from a political point of view the government must have its eyes on the provinces of central Canada. In fact I would go so far as to say that if a condition arose where the government had to make a choice as between the wishes of western Canada and the wishes of central Canada, its vote would be in favour of central Canada. It is an established fact that more than half the members in the Canadian House of Commons come from those two provinces.
We find that goods manufactured or produced1 at one point within the province of Alberta and transported' to another point bear a substantially higher rate than goods produced, let us say, at one point in Ontario and transported to another point within that same province where they are consumed. We find also that we suffer unfavourably from the point of view of distribution of goods within our province which are produced outside the province and brought into the province for consumption.
The particular situation which arises has already been referred to this evening. Goods which are manufactured in Ontario and shipped to Calgary or Edmonton bear a considerably higher freight charge than the same goods shipped to Vancouver. As an illustration, goods produced1 at Hamilton are shipped to Vancouver and then back to Calgary and sold more cheaply than they could be sold in the city of Vancouver.

subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Shipped back by local freight. I recall accompanying a merchant from my own town to Calgary. He was desirous of procuring a special type of grate for a furnace. We were told in Calgary that the only place the grate could be procured was in Vancouver. We pointed out that that seemed1 rather queer when the grate was manufactured in Hamilton. We were then told that it was found more profitable to establish a warehouse in Vancouver, ship the goods there to be stored, and then ship them by local freight to be sold in Alberta as they were required. Naturally such a situation creates a great deal of consternation among the consuming public of my province. It has already been pointed out that the kind of differential which creates that situation has caused Albertans to condemn the freight rate structure as it applies there.
We know what has happened in the past with regard to Alberta grain which went either to Winnipeg or to Vancouver. We know there is an eastern section of the province of Alberta
26G0
Freight Rates

where we reach the extreme apex of the freight rate structure. We realize less for the grain we produce there than is realized in any other part of Canada. This is due once again to the excessive freight charges which are imposed. Reference was also made to the situation west of Fort William where we find the breaking point at the head of the lakes and the constructive mileage principle which was introduced between Fort William and Winnipeg. This must be altered.
I have jotted down hastily a number of articles and I have indicated the increased freight dollars which we must pay as compared with the dollars paid by the consumer in Ontario. The previous speaker referred to automobiles. We find that for a Chrysler product produced in Windsor we have to pay $169 more than the consumer in Ontario. That is for a lower priced automobile, if there is such a thing left. In the medium priced field we find the difference running as high as $200. For a light delivery truck we pay $150 more per unit, and for a two-ton truck we pay as high as $227 more than the Ontario consumer.
On electric ranges we pay approximately $7 more, while refrigerators run from $6.25 to $12.75 more. Someone may suggest that that is not a very large sum, but when you multiply it by the number of such commodities consumed within our province you discover that the result is a large sum. In the case of the lowly washing machine we pay approximately $5 more.
As we have constantly emphasized, Mr. Farmer is penalized because he pays approximately $18 more for his binder than does the farmer in Ontario. His mower runs approximately $13 more, his ten-foot drill $10 or $15 more, his cream separator $23.50 more, his wagon $15 to $20 more. His 16 to 26-horsepower tractor $112 more; his power churn, which is used in the dairy industry in my province, $165 more than is paid by the Ontario farmer. I mention one other item, the bottle washing machine, which is also used in the dairy industry. It runs $130 more per unit than is paid in the province of Ontario. All these increases represent freight charges.
Let us take a few comparable figures of freight charges over comparable distances between central and western Canada. I find on making a comparison of the rates on first-class traffic, on standard mileage, for fifty miles we pay approximately three per cent more in Alberta; on the average 100-mile haul, 4-6 per cent more; on the 200-mile haul, 11-2 per cent more; on the 300-mile haul, 11*7 per cent more; on the 400-mile haul, 12 per cent more; on the 500-mile haul, 13-6

per cent more. If you apply those percentages to the actual freight moved in the course of a twelve-month period over those areas you will find that we are penalized extensively.
I have also a comparison of eastern and western ton-mile rates which are extremely illuminating. On grain we pay 13 per cent more per ton-mile than in central Canada; on flour and milk products the rate is equal; on lumber and squared timber, 31-1 per cent more per ton mile; on wood for fuel, 12-5 per cent more; on anthracite coal, 51-6 per cent more; on bituminous coal, 36-6 per cent more; on ores of various types, 30 per cent more; on livestock it is equal, also on dressed meats; on raw cotton, 5-3 per cent more; on other revenue billing, 15 per cent more.
The lumber situation has been referred to. Once again I have taken some comparable mileages in central Canada, and I find that on a carload of lumber hauled approximately 642 miles in Alberta we pay 85-1 per cent more. Lumber hauled in Alberta over a distance of 720 miles costs us 75 per cent more per car in freight; on 765 miles, 83 per cent more, and on 818 miles, 71-4 per cent more.
Here are a few more interesting figures. I do not care particularly to quote figures, but if they are given some consideration it will open the eyes of some of those who believe and say that we are crying with probably no justification.
A carload of lumber leaving the city of Edmonton and going to prairie points-I emphasize that, to prairie points-as compared with carloads of lumber moved within the two central provinces of Canada makes an interesting comparison. If we haul a car of lumber 244 miles on the prairies out of Edmonton we will pay 28-5 per cent more than they pay in the central provinces; on 294 miles, 23 per cent more; on 370 miles, 33-3 per cent more; on 425 miles, 20 per cent more; on 501 miles, 38-3 per cent more, and so on. I have other figures but I shall not give them.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) referred to fresh fruits and indicated that the growers of his province stand to lose hundreds of thousands if not a million dollars a year. Here are a few interesting figures. Let us take fresh fruit produced in his own area in British Columbia and shipped to our own province, as contrasted with fruits produced in the Hamilton area of this province and shipped to points in western Ontario or to any part of Ontario. On a haul of 301 miles we pay 38 per cent more than they pay in the province of Ontario; on a haul of 355 miles

Freight Rates
we pay as high as 60 per cent more; on a haul of 453 miles we pay 54 per cent more, and on a haul of 556 miles we pay 15-5 per cent more. You can imagine what the addition of 21 per cent to any of these figures which I have quoted will do to us and to business generally in western Canada. I repeat what I said before.
I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley was quite right in voicing the alarm he did voice a few moments ago.
Let us now look at a few general commodities which are used on the farm or in the home from day to day. Take shipments of commodities from eastern Canada to Vancouver and shipments of commodities from eastern Canada to Calgary or Edmonton in the province of Alberta. On soap alone we pay in freight in Calgary and Edmonton 98 per cent more than the consumer in the city of Vancouver; on twine, 79-6 per cent more; on wire, 164 per cent more than if that wire were shipped right through to the city of Vancouver; on calcium phosphate, 212-6 per cent more; on drugs and medicines, 102-3 per cent more; on lead, 164 per cent more; on boots and shoes, 51-8 per cent more; on linoleum and oil cloth, 58-4 per cent more; on wire rods, 138-6 per cent more; on window shades, 51-1 per cent more; on glass, 46-6 per cent more; on drygoods, 66-6 per cent more. I would emphasize that that is the increased rate per ton mile; it is important that I mention that.
There is a peculiar case which I have often mentioned. We have a condensery in my city of Red Deer. It produces the best canned or condensed milk produced anywhere in Canada. If we desire to ship that milk to Vancouver it has to compete with milk from Tillsonburg, Ontario, which is laid down in Vancouver much cheaper than we can lay down our Red Deer milk in Vancouver, purely because of the freight rate structure that prevails. If that is not a most discriminatory position I should like to have it explained. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, when we examine some of these figures that we hear more and more talk about the secession of the western provinces? In fact the talk is becoming in some instances extremely outspoken. I mentioned a moment ago that when these people look toward eastern Canada and attach a certain part of the responsibility to these two central provinces they may do so because of certain newspaper propaganda which circulated about the year 1907.
I think I quoted this once before but it might be well to put it on the record again. ' As I emphasized at that time, some people think this is the attitude which still prevails here, and until it is proven that this is not
the attitude, possibly we shall continue to believe that it is. This is from a newspaper of 1907:
The marvel of our west is its productiveness, the inrush of population, most of all the consuming capacity, the consuming possibility of that population for manufactured goods of all kinds. The farmers of the west do not haggle overprices, they have the money to buy all kinds of things, and with their rapidly increasing numbers they can support an immense population in some other portion of -the dominion better suited for industrial and manufacturing purposes.
Then the editorial goes on to indicate that the central provinces are the parts of Canada particularly adapted to profit from this large increase in population on the prairies. The people of western Canada-I presume the same is true of the maritime provinces also- are becoming a bit sick of the support which they are being constantly called upon to render to industry in central Canada. What central Canada will discover before too long is, I am quite sure, that the west will become highly industrialized, and then I presume it will not take them very long to tell central Canada just where they can go. The trend is in that direction, and unless some of these inequalities, inequities and disturbing conditions which prevail are removed that situation will develop just as surely as I stand here.
I for one am not questioning at the moment the necessity of the railroads for increased revenue. I prefer to leave that situation to the experts who are in possession of all the facts. However, I would be very much surprised if the government of Canada did not give careful consideration to one or two things which happened at the time of the application for an increase in freight rates. The first was that the Canadian Pacific made some extremely pessimistic estimates with respect to their operations, extremely pessimistic guesses, should I say. These estimates were not in any sense borne out by their own figures which later came to light. Let me say, secondly, if we are to adopt as a policy within this country that when demand starts falling off industry is to be permitted to jack its prices up, then I say you are guaranteeing to us one of the most disastrous depressions ever inflicted upon the Canadian people.
We hear government officials talking about production or competition lowering rates. I would like to see them give some encouragement to the carrying into effect of that bit of philosophy. No doubt the board of transport commissioners did what they were called upon to do. They examined the dollar position of the railroads; they examined the assertion that the railroads required additional revenues
Freight Rates

in order to carry on, and they recommended accordingly. I am not going to criticize the board of transport commissioners, but I say this: certainly, before they were ever called upon to authorize any increase in freight rates the government should have taken action to correct and remove the anomalies that existed within our present freight rate set-up.
I do not know why the government wait before doing a thing of that kind. They are now faced with a situation of this kind and they find themselves right up to their necks in hot water, squirming in every direction. I agree thoroughly with what has been said here today by speakers from every side of the house, that we should first establish an equalization of rates within this country in order that one part shall not be called upon to bear an unfair burden.
The government may wonder why this announcement caused such consternation. I hope they are conscious of some facts. I imagine the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows what it did out west, because I understand that he has been out there recently. This'increase of $70,000,000 in the cost of living at a time when our cost of living index shows that the cost of living is higher than it ever was in the history of Canada since the index was first established, coming on top [DOT]of such things as the coarse grain policy of last fall, the farmers' income tax forms, the excise taxes and so forth and so on, just seemed to bring everything to a head. I do not know, but it seems to me that this government have the uncanny faculty of doing things that bring condemnation down upon their heads; because if one looks back over the past four or five months he must conclude that, had they deliberately set about to do things to annoy the Canadian public they could not have been more successful than they have been. I am not going to say it was deliberate, because an election cannot be too far away; therefore I can hardly believe it would be deliberate. I would rather say they did the best they could, and it is simply that they were not equal to the task. That is about the only conclusion I can possibly come to.
I have been asked how long I am going to speak. I should speak until I have said what I started out to say, regardless of how long it takes. However, I am practically through. I speak for all of us over here, when I say that we join with those who demand that the government set aside, at least for the time being, the application of the 21 per cent increase, and that during the interim they set about to do what I am convinced they believe in their own hearts should be done, namely, a revision of

the whole Canadian freight rate structure. Only thus can you have a Canada that is prepared to talk in terms of Canada, and not a Canada parts of which are looking elsewhere for, I should not say relief, but at least for encouragement. I beseech the government to give consideration to what has been said here today and to take appropriate action forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks this
evening must of necessity be extremely brief, for reasons which I shall give in a moment. I would have welcomed very much the opportunity to participate in this debate at greater length than I am about to do. I would also have welcomed the opportunity to discuss some of the suggestions which have been made by hon. members this evening. In the first place, I think perhaps there may be some doubt as to whether or not this whole debate was in order. The matter of the freight rate question is, to my mind, still in the pending stage. However, if I had risen and taken that view there would have been a great deal of objection from the other side of the house and perhaps from this side as well. In any event I do not think it would have been well regarded in the country as a whole; therefore, for that reason, I withheld taking any technical objection to the motion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
There has been a tendency in this debate today to confuse two issues, the one which was the increase recommended by the board of transport commissioners and the other which was the equalization of the rates; or, to use the expression mentioned at various times in the debate, a discrimination in the rates across Canada.
I have listened carefully to the debate and have come to the conclusion that there has been a tendency to confuse those two issues. Those two issues are, I think, quite separate one from the other. The board in this case was dealing with one specific matter, namely an application, not by the government of Canada but by the railways, through the railway association of Canada representing some twenty railways, to the board of transport commissioners for an increase in freight rates.

I bring that to the attention of the house not because I do not regard with a great deal of sympathy what has been said by various members in connection with that very matter, but I did want to say simply this, that the two are distinct and separate matters, one not necessarily relying upon the other, although one may affect the other, as has been clearly stated this evening.
My hon. friend the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) stated that he did not object-I think I am paraphrasing his words- to an increase in freight rates as such, but that he objected to the inequalities which exist across the country. I do not wish to enter into a discussion of this and I said so at the outset; nor do I wish to be drawn into a discussion, for this reason, that there has been launched an intention to appeal by the maritime provinces, and I think, if it has not already been done, by the other provinces, save Ontario and Quebec. They have petitioned the governor in council that they intend to appeal the decision of the board, and I am afraid that anything I would say would be prejudging the case. I think, therefore, the house will understand that under the circumstances the best thing for me, or for that matter anyone speaking on behalf of the government, to do is simply to state that that petition, or that intention to appeal, has been launched. That being so, the petition will be dealt with when it is formally brought to the attention of the government. The chief point he raised was his contention that the question of discrimination was not part and parcel of the whole question of a general increase. He made out that because the application itself did not mention that, or did not make direct reference to the differentials or the discrimination, therefore the

I believe the question *was put directly to the minister while he was speaking, as to whether he did not think there was a connection between the two matters. If I understood him correctly, his opinion was that the question of discrimination or differentials would have to go by itself in a separate application before the board, before it could be properly considered. That, of course, is only an incidental. I am sure the minister must have a copy of the submissions of the Manitoba government in this matter. If he will turn to page 59 he will find that there is a summary of the previous decisions of the board. It goes back as far as 1914, and goes on to 1916, 1918, 1920, 1922 and 1927. In practically every case the decision by the board involved the question of differentials as to different parts of the country. For example, in 1917 there was an increase in the passenger and freight tolls, in what was called the 15 per cent case.
. . . there was a further recognition of the disparity between the east and the west-
I am quoting now from the submission.
-and in that case the western rates were raised 10 per cent only, whereas the general bulk of eastern rates were raised 15 per cent.
That in itself is an admission that the board was quite competent to take into consideration all the factors that go into the making of freight rates. Surely in the evidence that was given before the board of transport commissioners there were plenty of arguments to show that there was discrimination and that there was need for an overhaul of the system of freight rates in itself. I believe the board

Freight Rates
was quite competent to make that recommendation or that change. But the question that is still left hanging in the air is this: What is the government going to do in this matter on its own responsibility?
Many of us were anxious all during the session last year, and in the session so far this year, to say something in the house about this question, but we were prevented from doing so by the rules of the house inasmuch as the matter was then before the board, and it was ruled that it was of the same nature as being before the courts. We felt that at the first opportunity which presented itself we would get from the Minister of Transport, who, after all, is most closely connected with this matter, a full explanation of all the factors which went into the making of this decision. I believe the house is entitled to that sort of statement, and the country is certainly anxious to have it. All one has to do is to look through the headlines of the newspapers across Canada, since the -decision was rendered, and he will see that the people of Canada are anxious to know the basis on which that decision was arrived at; if the government-which, after all, has the final responsibility-is in favour of the decision made; and if not, what is it going to do about the matter? Yet all we get from the minister today is a brief and sketchy statement saying that in his opinion there are two matters involved, and that we must not confuse them.

If it is within the rules and within the rights of the members on this side of the house and of all private
members on the other side of the house to make arguments and submissions either to justify .the increase or to take the opposite stand-as we in this group have taken-then surely it is also within the competence of the minister. Surely he has just as many privileges in this house as has any other member and he should not feel backward or bashful. He is generally not bashful in this house, but on this .occasion he appears to shy away from the question and try to leave it hanging in the air.
Time will not permit me, Mr. Speaker, to say all the things I wanted to say in the first place, because it is now almost eleven o'clock. I only wish to say that I concur most heartily with what the leader of this group said; and I believe he has performed a public service to this country in raising the question today. I am disappointed, and I am sure the house generally is too, that the minister did not rise to the occasion to justify the action taken by the board.
